title: Unconditional Security Of Discrete-Modulated Cv-qkd From Infinite-Dimensional Meat
authors: Lars Kamin, Ian George, John Burniston, Florian Kanitschar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discrete-Modulated (DM) Continuous-Variable (CV) Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is an experimentally attractive approach to quantum cryptography, offering high key rates over metropolitan-scale distances while relying on state-of-the-art telecom infrastructure. However, a fundamental gap has remained between this experimental promise and rigorous security: for more than two decades, DM CV-QKD has lacked a complete composable finite-size security proof against coherent attacks. Existing works either restrict the adversary to collective attacks, impose additional finite-dimensional assumptions, apply only to specific modulation formats, or fail to recover the known asymptotic rates. Here, we resolve this longstanding problem by establishing the first complete composable finite-size security proof for DM CV-QKD protocols against coherent attacks, incorporating imperfect detectors and both fixed- and variable-length protocol variants. Our proof introduces two central results of broader interest: an infinite-dimensional marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem (iMEAT) and a rigorous dimension-reduction technique that makes the infinite-dimensional security bounds numerically tractable. The resulting key rates recover the known asymptotic rates and outperform established finite-size bounds based on collective attacks, while yielding positive key rates beyond [MATH]km for experimentally relevant block sizes and parameters. Thus, our work closes a longstanding gap and places an experimentally attractive class of CV-QKD protocols on a rigorous composable security footing and provides a pathway towards their practical deployment.
tldr: The paper provides the first complete composable finite-size security proof for discrete-modulated continuous-variable QKD against coherent attacks, introducing an infinite-dimensional marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem and a dimension-reduction technique.
motivation: Discrete-modulated CV-QKD is experimentally attractive but lacked rigorous finite-size composable security against coherent attacks for over two decades, limiting its practical deployment.
method: The authors establish an infinite-dimensional marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem (iMEAT) and develop a dimension-reduction technique to make the infinite-dimensional security bounds numerically tractable, covering imperfect detectors and both fixed- and variable-length protocols.
result: The resulting key rates recover known asymptotic rates, outperform existing finite-size bounds based on collective attacks, and yield positive key rates over metropolitan-scale distances for relevant block sizes and parameters.
conclusion: This work closes a longstanding gap by placing experimentally attractive DM CV-QKD protocols on a rigorous composable security footing, paving the way for practical deployment.

title: Exact Work Characteristic Functions For Time-Dependent Bosonic Quadratic Hamiltonians
authors: R. N. P. Maia F. Nicacio
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive an exact analytical expression for the characteristic function of work in closed many-body bosonic systems governed by general time-dependent quadratic Hamiltonians. This is made possible by adopting a unified prescription in which all operators appearing in the characteristic function are treated as elements of the inhomogeneous Metaplectic group. The esulting expression involves a single symplectic matrix, a single phase-space displacement, and a single accumulated phase. It holds for any number of degrees of freedom, arbitrary time dependence of the quadratic Hamiltonian, and any initial thermal equilibrium state of the system. The formalism trades the explicit time-ordering problem associated with the unitary evolution for the determination of a symplectic path in phase space, from which the corresponding driving Hamiltonian can be reconstructed. We also discuss the generalization to arbitrary nonequilibrium initial states within the two-projective-measurement scheme for quantum work. The same construction yields Loschmidt echoes and mixed-state total phases. Using the derived characteristic function, we obtain formulas for the Helmholtz free energy, the Jarzynski equality, the mean work, the work variance, and the nonequilibrium lag. Undisplaced Hamiltonians, sudden quenches, constant-Hessian protocols, and the adiabatic limit follow as special cases of the general result. As an illustration, we analyze a one-dimensional system constructed from an unconventional symplectic path and exhibiting physically relevant limiting cases. We then show how affine and purely symplectic contributions affect work statistics and irreversibility.
tldr: The paper derives an exact analytical expression for the work characteristic function of closed many-body bosonic systems driven by arbitrary time-dependent quadratic Hamiltonians, valid for any number of modes and any initial thermal state.
motivation: Computing work statistics and fluctuation-theorem quantities for driven many-body quantum systems is generally obstructed by time-ordering and the complexity of the evolution, and exact results for general quadratic bosonic driving are lacking.
method: All operators in the characteristic function are treated as elements of the inhomogeneous Metaplectic group, reducing the time-ordered unitary evolution to a single symplectic path, a phase-space displacement, and an accumulated phase, with a two-projective-measurement scheme used to extend the result to arbitrary nonequilibrium initial states.
result: The formalism yields closed-form expressions for the Helmholtz free energy, the Jarzynski equality, mean work, work variance, and the nonequilibrium lag, and reproduces undisplaced Hamiltonians, sudden quenches, constant-Hessian protocols and the adiabatic limit as special cases; Loschmidt echoes and mixed-state total phases follow from the same construction.
conclusion: The work provides a unified, time-ordering-free framework for exact quantum work statistics in driven bosonic quadratic systems, clarifying how affine (displacement) and purely symplectic contributions shape work statistics and irreversibility.

title: Pump-Free Microwave-Optical Bell Pair Generation For Teleportation-Based Quantum Transduction
authors: Fangxin Li, Jaesung Heo, Zhaoyou Wang, Benjamin Pingault, Xingyu Gao, Tengyang Ruan, Anjun Chu, David D. Awschalom, Andrew N. Cleland, Andrew P. Higginbotham, Alexander A. High, Liang Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The coherent conversion between microwave and optical photons, known as quantum transduction, is critical for connecting superconducting processors to optical networks. Existing methods are limited by complications associated with optical pumping. We propose a pump-free microwave-optical Bell-pair source for teleportation-based transduction. Using a spin or atomic system resonantly coupled to optical and microwave cavities, the scheme generates loss-robust heralded Bell pairs. Across color centers, atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated systems, this assembly achieves kilohertz-range heralding rates with high fidelity.
tldr: The paper proposes a pump-free microwave-optical Bell-pair source for teleportation-based quantum transduction, using spin or atomic systems coupled to optical and microwave cavities.
motivation: Coherent microwave-optical transduction is essential for connecting superconducting quantum processors to optical networks, but existing methods suffer from complications related to optical pumping.
method: A spin or atomic system is resonantly coupled to optical and microwave cavities to generate loss-robust heralded Bell pairs, avoiding optical pumping, and the scheme is analyzed across color centers, atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated systems.
result: The assembly achieves kilohertz-range heralding rates with high fidelity across the considered platforms.
conclusion: This pump-free approach offers a promising route for teleportation-based quantum transduction between microwave and optical photons.

The central idea is to generate heralded Bell pairs between a microwave photon and an optical photon via a spontaneous Raman process, avoiding the need for an external optical pump that typically introduces noise and heating. The scheme is designed to be loss-robust, meaning that the heralding signal ensures the presence of the Bell pair even in the presence of photon loss. The authors analyze the performance across three physical platforms: color centers (e.g., nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond), atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated systems (e.g., optomechanical or electro-optomechanical devices). They report that the assembly can achieve kilohertz-range heralding rates with high fidelity, making it potentially suitable for teleportation-based transduction between superconducting quantum processors and optical networks. The paper is largely theoretical, providing a detailed protocol and rate analysis, but does not present experimental implementation.

title: Environmental Records Unlock Universal Quantum Computation From Thermal Decoherence
authors: Qi Zhao Chenfeng Cao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: At a fixed thermal exposure, the same stabilizer processor can be classically simulable or quantum universal, depending on which environmental records its controller retains. We give an exact computational classification of energy-counting thermal-idle instruments in a quantum processor with ideal stabilizer control and independent local Markov baths. The relaxation time [MATH], homogeneous coherence time [MATH], and equilibrium excited-state population [MATH] determine an exact computational boundary at [MATH]. If every location lies at or below it, branchwise nonnegative stabilizer decompositions give an explicit efficient classical sampler for the adaptive circuit and its full time-resolved exchange record. Above it at a single repeatedly accessible location, a suitable idle duration and no-exchange conditioning supply distillable ancillas and enable universal quantum computation with polynomial overhead. At finite temperature on the resource side, erasing the record at a sufficiently long, unsplit exposure makes the averaged channel stabilizer measure-and-prepare, and even a terminal parity check then yields only simulable branches. Yet at that same exposure, retaining only the bit recording whether any exchange occurred still heralds distillable ancillas, because a thermal round trip restores the parity after its first exchange has already removed the coherence.
tldr: Thermal decoherence in a stabilizer processor can be either classically simulable or quantum universal depending on which environmental records the controller retains, with an exact computational boundary set by relaxation, coherence, and equilibrium excited-state population.
motivation: To understand how thermal idle dynamics and environmental record-keeping determine the computational power of a quantum processor.
method: Models energy-counting thermal-idle instruments with ideal stabilizer control and independent local Markov baths, deriving branchwise nonnegative stabilizer decompositions and record-conditioned channels.
result: Below the boundary an efficient classical sampler exists; above it at one repeatedly accessible location, distillable ancillas enable universal quantum computation with polynomial overhead, while retaining only an exchange bit can still herald distillable ancillas even when erasing the record yields simulable branches.
conclusion: Environmental records from thermal decoherence are a computational resource that can unlock universality, linking thermodynamic exposure to quantum computational capability.

title: A Complete Classification Of The Existence Of Finite-dimensional Quantum Solutions To Inconsistent Linear Constraint Systems
authors: Markus Frembs
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear constraint systems (LCS) provide a compact algebraic language for nonlocal games and state-independent contextuality. In the binary case the Mermin--Peres square shows that inconsistent LCS can be solved by promoting variables to local Pauli operators, whereas a series of no-go results excludes analogous Pauli-, Clifford- and monomial unitary-based constructions at odd prime modulus. We first isolate the reason for this difference: for tensor-product quantum solutions, the obstruction to a classical solution of a LCS over [MATH] decomposes into obstruction classes carried by the individual factors. As a consequence, a genuinely global obstruction cannot arise solely by tensoring locally unobstructed systems. The argument is specific to odd modulus; at even modulus the reordering phase need not vanish, as in Pauli-based examples. Given this distinction, we instead associate LCS to finite arrangements of rank-one projectors and resolutions of the identity in finite-dimensional vector spaces. Quantum solvability for such LCS is automatic and the search for a quantum-classical gap rests entirely on proving classical unsatisfiability of the underlying modular incidence problem of the arrangement. By relating such LCS with group-valued frame functions, we identify a family of examples in the work of [Harding, Jager, and Smith, Int. J. Theor. Phys. 44, 539 (2005)]. To establish the (non)existence of classically unsatisfiable LCS over [MATH] with quantum solutions in all dimensions [MATH] and for all [MATH], we further construct explicit examples for the cases [MATH] prime. Our main result thus positively resolves the existence problem of such LCS beyond the binary case: such systems exist if and only if [MATH] and [MATH]. Moreover, we establish the existence of LCS with a quantum-classical gap over finite fields if and only if [MATH] and [MATH].
tldr: The paper completely classifies when inconsistent linear constraint systems admit finite-dimensional quantum solutions, showing existence if and only if specific arithmetic conditions hold and establishing quantum-classical gaps over finite fields.
motivation: Linear constraint systems provide a compact algebraic framework for nonlocal games and state-independent contextuality, but prior no-go results left open when quantum solutions exist beyond the binary Mermin-Peres square.
method: The author decomposes obstructions for tensor-product quantum solutions into factor-wise classes, associates LCS to arrangements of rank-one projectors and resolutions of identity, connects them to group-valued frame functions, and constructs explicit examples for prime-modulus cases.
result: A global obstruction cannot arise solely by tensoring locally unobstructed systems, quantum solvability for projector arrangements is automatic, and the main theorem gives necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of such LCS and of quantum-classical gaps over finite fields.
conclusion: This work resolves the existence problem for inconsistent LCS with finite-dimensional quantum solutions beyond the binary case, providing a complete classification and new examples of contextuality/nonlocality.

This decomposition relies on the vanishing of a reordering phase that holds only for odd modulus. The authors then shift to a geometric approach, associating LCS with finite arrangements of rank-one projectors and resolutions of the identity. In this setting, quantum solvability is automatic, and the quantum-classical gap reduces to classical unsatisfiability of a modular incidence problem. title: The Transient Counting Statistics Of Autonomous Quantum Clocks
authors: Sreenath K. Manikandan Oscar Arandes
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: At the heart of every atomic clock is a quantum coherent emitter, the laser, that could in principle be treated autonomously. While their frequency or phase stability is typically studied in the semiclassical regime of a large number of emitted quanta, recent works on autonomous quantum clocks suggest that the few-quanta regime can offer statistical information in the temporal domain. This provides complementary means to probe the fundamental limits to precise timekeeping in the quantum regime. Motivated by these works, we consider simple models for two- and three-level quantum emitters subject to an athermal fueling through dephasing, which generically results in coherences in the steady state. A large deviation principle with finite-time contributions is used to identify the transient counting statistics and their dependence on the initial conditions. We conclude by discussing the implications for precise timekeeping and quantum sensing using autonomous quantum emitters as clocks in their transient regime.
tldr: The paper analyzes the transient counting statistics of autonomous quantum clocks using simple two- and three-level emitters with athermal dephasing, revealing fundamental limits to timekeeping precision in the few-quanta regime.
motivation: Recent works suggest that the few-quanta regime of autonomous quantum clocks offers statistical temporal information that could probe fundamental limits to precise timekeeping, complementing semiclassical studies.
method: The authors consider two- and three-level quantum emitters subject to athermal fueling through dephasing and apply a large deviation principle with finite-time contributions to characterize the transient counting statistics and their dependence on initial conditions.
result: They identify the transient counting statistics and show how athermal dephasing generically leads to coherences in the steady state, with the statistics depending on the initial conditions.
conclusion: The findings have implications for precise timekeeping and quantum sensing using autonomous quantum emitters as clocks in their transient regime.

The study aims to connect autonomous quantum clock models with quantum sensing protocols, suggesting that transient counting statistics can provide complementary information for precise timekeeping. The analysis is primarily theoretical, using master equations and large deviation theory to derive the statistics of photon emissions. The paper concludes by discussing implications for quantum sensing and the role of coherences in enhancing temporal precision.

title: Utility-Based Path Selection And Configuration In Quantum Networks Via Layered Shortest Paths
authors: Leonardo Bacciottini, Subhransu Maji, Don Towsley, Gayane Vardoyan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A path in a quantum network is a chain of repeaters that distributes entanglement between two users. Selecting a path requires balancing the rate and quality (e.g., fidelity) of the delivered entanglement, but these quantities, unlike standard routing metrics, compose non-additively. The problem is compounded by link-level configuration choices (e.g., distillation rounds or emitter brightness tuning), each trading rate against fidelity, so that a path's performance depends jointly on its route and its per-link settings. We cast this joint path selection and configuration problem as a shortest path computation on a layered graph whose layers track discretized end-to-end fidelity. A single run returns the full rate fidelity Pareto frontier, from which the path maximizing any nondecreasing utility function of rate and fidelity can be selected. We prove that for certain utility functions (including the secret key rate of BB84), the method is a fully polynomial time approximation scheme, returning a near-optimal path within a specified tolerance. We further characterize exactly when cheaper scalarization-based routing suffices: it is optimal for utility functions with convex fidelity profiles, but can be arbitrarily suboptimal otherwise (e.g., for step-like, sigmoidal utilities), whereas the layered method remains reliable in all cases.
tldr: The paper formulates joint path selection and link configuration in quantum networks as a layered shortest path problem that yields the rate-fidelity Pareto frontier and near-optimal paths for utility functions.
motivation: Selecting an entanglement distribution path requires balancing rate and fidelity, but these metrics compose non-additively and interact with per-link configuration choices such as distillation rounds or emitter brightness.
method: The authors build a layered graph whose layers track discretized end-to-end fidelity and compute shortest paths to recover the full rate-fidelity Pareto frontier, then prove an FPTAS for certain utility functions and characterize when scalarization-based routing is sufficient.
result: The layered method returns a near-optimal path within a specified tolerance for utilities including the BB84 secret key rate, while scalarization is optimal only for convex fidelity profiles and can be arbitrarily suboptimal for step-like or sigmoidal utilities.
conclusion: The approach provides a reliable utility-based routing and configuration framework for quantum networks and clarifies the limits of simpler scalarization-based routing.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the problem of joint path selection and link configuration in quantum networks, where entanglement distribution requires balancing rate and fidelity. Unlike classical routing metrics, these quantities compose non-additively along a path, and each link has configuration choices (e.g., distillation rounds, emitter brightness) that trade rate for fidelity. The authors formulate this as a shortest path computation on a layered graph, where layers correspond to discretized end-to-end fidelity. A single run of their algorithm returns the full rate-fidelity Pareto frontier, enabling selection of the path that maximizes any nondecreasing utility function of rate and fidelity. They prove that for certain utility functions, including the secret key rate of BB84, the method is a fully polynomial time approximation scheme (FPTAS), guaranteeing a near-optimal path within a specified tolerance. They also characterize when simpler scalarization-based routing suffices: it is optimal for utility functions with convex fidelity profiles but can be arbitrarily suboptimal for non-convex profiles (e.g., step-like or sigmoidal utilities), whereas the layered method remains reliable in all cases.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The core methodological innovation is the transformation of the joint routing and configuration problem into a shortest path search on a layered graph. Each layer represents a discretized level of end-to-end fidelity, and edges encode both the physical link and its configuration choices, with weights corresponding to rate (or a function thereof). By discretizing fidelity, the authors convert the non-additive composition of fidelity into an additive path metric within the layered structure. The algorithm computes the Pareto frontier of rate and fidelity by finding, for each fidelity layer, the maximum achievable rate. This frontier is then used to select the optimal path for any nondecreasing utility function. The FPTAS property is established by relating the discretization granularity to the approximation guarantee, ensuring polynomial running time in the input size and the inverse of the tolerance. The analysis of scalarization-based routing compares the convexity of the utility function's fidelity profile to the geometry of the Pareto frontier, proving optimality for convex cases and constructing adversarial examples for non-convex cases.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper's key theoretical results include: (1) the layered graph algorithm returns the full rate-fidelity Pareto frontier in a single run, with complexity polynomial in the network size and the inverse of the fidelity discretization step; (2) for utility functions such as the BB84 secret key rate, the algorithm is an FPTAS, meaning it finds a path within a factor (1+ε) of optimal in time polynomial in 1/ε; (3) scalarization-based routing is optimal if and only if the utility function's fidelity profile is convex, and can be arbitrarily suboptimal otherwise—the authors provide examples where the performance gap is unbounded. The characterization of scalarization's limitations is particularly significant, as it identifies a fundamental pitfall in common routing approaches for quantum networks.

The layered graph approach elegantly handles the non-additive composition of fidelity and rate, enabling efficient computation of the Pareto frontier.
Clearly delineates the conditions under which simpler scalarization methods are sufficient, offering actionable guidance for network designers.

title: Hidden Kinetic Correlations Control Collective Phases Of Entropy-conditioned Histories
authors: Abhishek Chowdhury
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Visible dynamics and mean dissipation need not determine the collective phases of rare histories. We construct local Markov models with identical ordinary visible path distributions, stationary states, mean entropy production, mean jump activity and driving affinities, yet different phases when histories are weighted by their full entropy production. Visible configurations modulate hidden driven cycles, whose exact elimination turns kinetic correlations into interactions. A positive spectral reduction separates hidden relaxation from collective modes. Periodic binary models retain opposite phases with entropy variances matched at every observation time. For conserved particles, a pair matches the first two joint cumulants of entropy and hidden activity at every observation time, yet selects segregation or a fluctuating state with suppressed long-wavelength density noise. Bound-state transport and fermionic evolution determine their contrasting dynamics. At a clean Ising critical midpoint, the entropy source couples quadratically to the thermal perturbation, making the fourth cumulant the first to detect the critical susceptibility. Its rate per site grows logarithmically, with an exact cutoff set by system size and observation time. For two quenched disorder ensembles, exact sample-response formulas and numerical evidence support a finite fourth-cumulant density despite very slow relaxation; a weak-disorder continuum response admits a controlled Borel sum. A common positive hidden eigenvector characterizes autonomous selected dynamics. When this condition fails, a finite network develops visible memory while preserving its ordinary visible process and mean diagnostics. These results identify kinetic information missed by aggregate thermodynamic observations.
tldr: Hidden kinetic correlations in stochastic dynamics can control collective phases of entropy-conditioned histories even when standard thermodynamic and visible process observables are identical.
motivation: Aggregate thermodynamic quantities like mean entropy production are often assumed to characterize dissipation and dynamics, but rare histories weighted by their full entropy production may reveal hidden kinetic information missed by such averages.
method: The paper constructs local Markov models with hidden driven cycles, uses exact elimination and a positive spectral reduction to separate hidden relaxation from collective modes, and analyzes entropy-conditioned history phases, criticality, and disorder responses.
result: Identical visible statistics and mean diagnostics can yield opposite entropy-conditioned phases; hidden kinetic correlations produce collective segregation, suppressed long-wavelength density noise, and critical detection via the fourth cumulant with logarithmic growth and disorder-dependent finite density.
conclusion: These results identify kinetic information missed by aggregate thermodynamic observations and provide a framework for understanding hidden correlations in nonequilibrium collective dynamics.

The authors construct local Markov models where hidden driven cycles are modulated by visible configurations; eliminating these hidden degrees of freedom exactly generates kinetic interactions. A positive spectral reduction separates hidden relaxation from collective modes, enabling the analysis of phase transitions in the ensemble of histories weighted by full entropy production. For periodic binary models, they demonstrate opposite phases with entropy variances matched at every observation time. For conserved particles, they find a pair of models that match the first two joint cumulants of entropy and hidden activity at all times, yet one selects segregation while the other exhibits a fluctuating state with suppressed long-wavelength density noise. Bound-state transport and fermionic evolution are shown to govern these contrasting dynamics. At a clean Ising critical midpoint, the entropy source couples quadratically to the thermal perturbation, making the fourth cumulant the first to detect the critical susceptibility; its rate per site grows logarithmically with an exact cutoff set by system size and observation time. For two quenched disorder ensembles, exact sample-response formulas and numerical evidence support a finite fourth-cumulant density despite very slow relaxation, and a weak-disorder continuum response admits a controlled Borel sum. Finally, a common positive hidden eigenvector characterizes autonomous selected dynamics; when this condition fails, a finite network develops visible memory while preserving its ordinary visible process and mean diagnostics.

Introduces a positive spectral reduction that separates hidden relaxation from collective modes, enabling the identification of phase transitions in the history ensemble and providing a framework for analyzing kinetic information beyond aggregate observables.

Shows that for conserved particles, matching the first two joint cumulants of entropy and hidden activity at all observation times is insufficient to determine the phase; segregation versus fluctuating states with suppressed long-wavelength density noise can arise from bound-state transport and fermionic evolution.

At a clean Ising critical midpoint, finds that the entropy source couples quadratically to the thermal perturbation, making the fourth cumulant the first to detect critical susceptibility, with a rate per site growing logarithmically and an exact cutoff set by system size and observation time.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of exact analytical constructions and spectral methods. They build local Markov jump models with hidden states that are driven by visible configurations, then eliminate the hidden degrees of freedom to obtain effective dynamics for the visible variables. This elimination turns kinetic correlations into interactions, which are analyzed using a positive spectral reduction that separates fast hidden relaxation from slow collective modes. The spectral reduction likely involves a similarity transformation or a decomposition of the generator into a part with positive spectrum and a part describing collective behavior. For specific models, they compute exact cumulants of entropy and hidden activity, and use generating functions to match these cumulants across different models. The analysis of the Ising critical midpoint uses scaling arguments and exact calculations of the fourth cumulant, with logarithmic growth and cutoff determined by finite size and observation time. For disordered systems, they derive exact sample-response formulas and perform numerical simulations to support the existence of a finite fourth-cumulant density, and they use Borel summation to handle the weak-disorder continuum response. The methodology is mathematically rigorous, combining probability theory, statistical mechanics, and spectral analysis.

title: Noise-induced Classical Phases In Optimally-unraveled Random Quantum Circuits
authors: Lorenzo Fioroni, Filippo Ferrari, Emanuele Tirrito
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the classical simulability of open quantum dynamics using random Clifford circuits doped with non-Clifford phase rotations and subject to local noise. We unravel the dynamics into stochastic quantum trajectories simulated with Clifford-augmented matrix product states, and introduce a simulation cost that quantifies the classical resources required. Optimizing this cost over stochastic unravelings, we identify noise-induced classical phases: extended parameter regions in which the dynamics can be fully disentangled by Clifford operations at arbitrary circuit depth. Their existence depends on both the noise model the unraveling. Using a geometric representation of quantum channels, we analytically determine optimal unravelings for a broad class of noise models, with numerical simulations confirming the predicted phase boundaries. We further relate the optimal cost to the unraveling-independent nonstabilizerness of the channel and show that, together with trajectory-resolved entanglement and nonstabilizerness, it classifies distinct dynamical regimes. Finally, we show that these classical phases disappear in the averaged density-matrix description, where no unraveling freedom remains. Our results show that the emergence of classicality in noisy random circuits depends on the measurement scheme adopted to probe it, and paves the way to further studies on the classical simulability of driven-dissipative dynamics.
tldr: The paper identifies noise-induced classical phases in noisy random Clifford circuits by optimizing stochastic unravelings and quantifying classical simulation cost.
motivation: Understanding when noisy open quantum dynamics becomes classically simulable and how the chosen unraveling affects the emergence of classicality.
method: Clifford-augmented matrix product state simulation of stochastic quantum trajectories is combined with a geometric channel representation to optimize simulation cost and relate it to nonstabilizerness and entanglement.
result: Extended classical phases exist where dynamics are fully disentanglable by Clifford operations at arbitrary depth, depending on noise model and unraveling, and disappear in the averaged density-matrix description.
conclusion: The emergence of classicality in noisy random circuits is measurement-scheme dependent, providing a resource-theoretic classification of dynamical regimes and implications for driven-dissipative simulability.

Using a geometric representation of quantum channels, the authors analytically determine optimal unravelings for a broad class of noise models, and numerical simulations confirm the predicted phase boundaries. Finally, they demonstrate that these classical phases disappear in the averaged density-matrix description, where no unraveling freedom remains. The results highlight that the emergence of classicality in noisy random circuits depends on the measurement scheme adopted to probe it, and open avenues for studying the classical simulability of driven-dissipative dynamics.

title: Strong Converse For The Quantum Capacity Of The Pure-loss Bosonic Channel
authors: Mark M. Wilde
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper reports the proof of a strong converse for the unconstrained quantum capacity of the pure-loss bosonic channel. At every fixed rate above capacity, the entanglement-generation fidelity of every code is bounded by a constant times the reciprocal of the number of channel uses. The bound holds without an energy constraint and for arbitrary encoded states, including states correlated across all input modes, and arbitrary joint decoders. The proof combines quantum Chebyshev and hockey-stick testing inequalities with a uniform relative-entropy-variance bound for the balanced pure-loss channel, corresponding to transmissivity [MATH]. The variance bound follows by expressing the balanced beam splitter in bright and dark modes: the dark modes are exactly in vacuum, and any state orthogonal to that vacuum contains at least one dark photon. For general transmissivity, dilating the degrading attenuator reduces the problem to this balanced-channel setting and bounds the decoder test by precisely the factor that produces the known quantum-capacity threshold. The resulting argument establishes the strong converse at the unconstrained quantum capacity for every pure-loss bosonic channel.

method: Combines quantum Chebyshev and hockey-stick testing inequalities with a uniform relative-entropy variance bound for the balanced pure-loss channel, using bright/dark mode decomposition and attenuator dilation.
result: For every fixed rate above capacity, the entanglement-generation fidelity of any code is bounded by a constant divided by the number of channel uses, holding for arbitrary encoded states and joint decoders.
conclusion: Establishes the strong converse at the unconstrained quantum capacity for every pure-loss bosonic channel, solidifying the capacity threshold.

title: Coupling Structure Determines Communication Regimes In Discrete Quantum Convolutional Channels
authors: Chunhe Xiong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the recently developed theory of quantum convolution for discrete-variable quantum systems. We classify the discrete quantum convolutional channels generated by an invertible [MATH] coupling matrix and a fixed environmental state according to which entries of the coupling ma- trix vanish. Under role-preserving basis relabelings, matrices with all four entries nonzero form [MATH] canonical cross-ratio classes, whereas matrices with exactly one vanishing entry split into four inequivalent branches. We determine the optimized one-shot Holevo information and the classical, quantum, and private capacities for all four one-entry-vanishing branches. If a diago- nal entry vanishes, the channel is an entanglement-breaking measure-and-prepare orbit channel: its classical capacity equals a relative entropy coherence of the environmental state, whereas its quantum and private capacities vanish. If an off-diagonal entry vanishes, the channel is a degradable generalized-dephasing channel: one complete orthonormal basis is transmitted without error, whereas the quantum and private capacities are determined by the entropy deficit of the environ-ental state after dephasing in the conjugate basis. Thus, the position of a single vanishing entry selects two qualitatively different communication regimes. When all four entries are nonzero, the channels are irreducibly Weyl covariant, reducing the classical-capacity problem to a regularized minimum-output-entropy problem. For the unique fully nonzero coupling class in the single-qutrit case, we further derive an exact Holevo formula for a depolarized one-parameter family and identify its entanglement-breaking threshold.

title: Phantom Codes: Hardness, Rate Optimal qLDPC Constructions, And Distance Limits

abstract: ArXiv:2609.16542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An [MATH] stabilizer code is phantom if every in-block logical CNOT gate can be realized by a permutation of its physical qubits. This eliminates the large and complicated physical overhead normally required for logical entangling gates. Yet this symmetry is highly restrictive: phantom codes are rare, the number of logical qubits is limited to [MATH], and no phantom qLDPC family with growing logical dimension was previously known. We make three contributions. 1. We prove that recognizing phantomness of a given stabilizer code is at least as hard as Graph Isomorphism, even for CSS codes encoding only [MATH] logical qubits. 2. We propose the first rate optimal phantom qLDPC families: for every fixed [MATH], our CSS families achieve the maximal logical scaling [MATH] and distance [MATH]. 3. We prove a distance no-go theorem: every phantom code family with [MATH] and check weight [MATH] satisfies [MATH] for sufficiently large [MATH]. Thus our fixed-distance qLDPC families are distance-scaling optimal at the maximal logical scaling [MATH].

title: Error-corrected Function Estimation Advantage In Multiparameter Hamiltonians
authors: Erfan Abbasgholinejad, Lorc\'an O. Conlon, Sean R. Muleady, Jacob Bringewatt, Ali Fahimniya, Yu-Xin Wang, Alexey V. Gorshkov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish the ultimate precision limits for estimating a function of multiple Hamiltonian parameters in the presence of Markovian noise. By reducing multiparameter function estimation to an optimization over effective single-parameter embeddings, we derive tight bounds on the quantum Fisher information. We identify a necessary and sufficient functional Hamiltonian-not-in-Lindblad-span condition for Heisenberg-limited scaling in time. When this condition holds, we construct a code that simultaneously removes the noise and nuisance Hamiltonian parameters while preserving the target signal. When it fails, we derive the optimal standard quantum-limit coefficient and show that it is asymptotically attainable using approximate quantum error correction. Finally, we demonstrate that direct function estimation can substantially outperform estimating all parameters individually and subsequently evaluating the function. This advantage can scale with both the evolution time and the number of parameters.

title: Hyperbolic Color Codes With Constant Rate And Polynomial Distance
authors: Hayata Yamasaki Shun Hasegawa
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in quantum hardware relax the strict geometric-locality constraints traditionally imposed on quantum error-correcting codes, motivating interest in high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. At the same time, color codes provide a particularly rich setting for fault-tolerant quantum computation, underlying protocols such as single-shot error correction and self-correcting quantum computation. Hyperbolic color codes provide a class of high-rate qLDPC codes that also retain the structural features of color codes relevant to fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, previous constructions of hyperbolic color codes have achieved at most logarithmic code distance. In this work, we construct hyperbolic color codes with both constant rate and polynomial distance by building on arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds that support polynomial-distance hyperbolic toric codes. Our construction applies in arbitrary dimension \(D\geq 4\). In even dimensions, the resulting type-\(D/2\) color codes have constant encoding rate and polynomial distance, while in other cases the number of logical qubits and the code distance both exhibit polynomial scaling. We further derive explicit exponents for polynomial lower bounds as functions of the dimension and code type. These results establish a family of hyperbolic color codes simultaneously achieving constant rate and polynomial distance and providing a testbed to explore fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols that combine high-rate quantum codes with the structural advantages of color codes.

title: Towards Block-Level Fault-Tolerant Quantum Simulation On Small High-Rate Non-CSS Codes
authors: Narayanan Rengaswamy Zhuangzhuang Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small high-rate non-CSS stabilizer codes provide compact platforms for encoded quantum computation, but mixed-Pauli checks and limited native transversal logical gates complicate fault-tolerant dynamics. Block-level constructions offer an alternative by mapping an entire logical block to a physical circuit rather than compiling separately protected logical gates. We investigate this approach using the high-rate [[8,3,3]] non-CSS code and logical Trotter circuits as a testbed. We construct flagged syndrome-extraction circuits and establish a circuit-level memory pseudo-threshold near \(1.5\times10^{-3}\). We then apply our symplectic-transvection construction, which maps a logical Trotter circuit to a physical circuit with the same block pattern for any stabilizer code. Although this mapping preserves the intended unitary algebraically, encoded Trotter circuits exhibit asymmetry between logical-\(X\) and logical-\(Z\) failure channels. Single-fault analysis identifies the mechanism: a fault on the shared parity ancilla can propagate through the uncomputation network into an undetectable logical operator, reducing the effective circuit distance in the affected sector. We evaluate flag-conditioned recovery, biased-noise decoding, CliNR resource verification, flag postselection, and asymmetric gate-noise models. These methods suppress propagated faults but do not simultaneously suppress both logical sectors in the realistic configurations studied. A diagnostic protected limit removing the identified malignant first-order locations restores pseudo-threshold behavior in both sectors, approaching memory performance. These results demonstrate the potential of block-level logical constructions for non-CSS codes without rich native transversal gate sets and the joint protection of the parity network, analog rotation, and recovery required to preserve fault-tolerant distance.

conclusion: Block-level logical constructions show potential for non-CSS codes without rich native transversal gate sets, but preserving fault-tolerant distance requires joint protection of the parity network, analog rotation, and recovery.

title: Pulse-Level Compilation Of Measurement-Free Recovery In Transmon Circuits
authors: Yi-Han Yu, Kai Xu, Heng Fan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error correction commonly relies on syndrome measurement, decoding, and conditional feedback. We numerically show that the conditional spectrum of an interacting transmon circuit can compile a local recovery rule into a fixed open-loop control cycle. In a four-bit repetition-code ring, the resulting input-independent control slows the decay of logical coherence under Pauli-\(X\) noise and stabilizes logical-one population under data relaxation relative to uncorrected references. Its local, bounded-degree architecture provides a hardware-native framework for extending compiled recovery control to larger quantum networks.
tldr: Numerically demonstrates pulse-level compilation of measurement-free recovery in a four-bit transmon repetition-code ring, slowing logical coherence decay under Pauli-X noise.
motivation: Quantum error correction commonly relies on syndrome measurement, decoding, and conditional feedback, which can be challenging to implement at the hardware level.
method: The authors use the conditional spectrum of an interacting transmon circuit to compile a local recovery rule into a fixed open-loop control cycle, tested on a four-bit repetition-code ring.
result: The input-independent control slows the decay of logical coherence under Pauli-X noise and stabilizes logical-one population under data relaxation relative to uncorrected references.
conclusion: The work provides a hardware-native, local bounded-degree framework for extending compiled recovery control to larger quantum networks.

title: Error-Bounded Fixed-Point Design Of Super-Sample-Rate Iir Filters For Real-Time Superconducting Qubit Flux Predistortion
authors: Matt Huszabianlou, Angelos Ioannou, Nirmalendu Bikash Patra, Anastasiia Butko, Gang Huang, Irfan Siddiqi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flux-activated two-qubit gates in superconducting processors require correction of line distortion, which otherwise produces residual detuning, conditional-phase error, and leakage. Prior demonstrations of cryoscope-based distortion calibration have generally used commercial solutions that specify the filter models but not their FPGA implementation. These details matter for custom and open-source systems, where the fixed-point coefficient and datapath formats set how accurately the correction is realized, and the IIR feedback loop in its standard form does not meet timing at the required clock rate. We derive the coefficient formats of the correction filters from a step response error tolerance, using bounds on the quantization-induced displacement of the poles and zeros over the physical parameter range of each distortion, and the accumulator format from the smallest input change that must remain resolvable at the output. The same analysis gives the conditions under which quantization preserves filter stability. We implement the resulting FIR/IIR cascade on the QubiC platform at a fabric clock rate of {MHz}, using a super-sample-rate structure with scattered look-ahead pipelining, which removes the feedback recursion from the critical path without changing the target transfer function. A representative cascade for our {GS/s} flux lines, comprising an integrator, a second-order section, and a 20-tap FIR, consumes 88 DSP slices and adds {ns} of latency. We confirm the hardware implementation by correcting characteristic bias-tee distortion, an intermediate step toward full cryoscope-based calibration.
tldr: This paper presents a fixed-point design methodology for super-sample-rate IIR filters used in real-time flux predistortion for superconducting qubits, implemented on the QubiC platform.
motivation: Flux-activated two-qubit gates in superconducting processors require correction of line distortion, but prior cryoscope-based calibration relies on commercial solutions that obscure FPGA implementation details critical for custom and open-source systems.
method: The authors derive coefficient formats from step response error tolerance using quantization-induced pole-zero displacement bounds, and implement a FIR/IIR cascade with scattered look-ahead pipelining to remove the feedback recursion from the critical path.
result: A representative cascade for 1 GS/s flux lines, comprising an integrator, a second-order section, and a 20-tap FIR, consumes 88 DSP slices and adds only a few nanoseconds of latency, successfully correcting characteristic bias-tee distortion.
conclusion: The work enables accurate, stable fixed-point filter design for custom superconducting qubit control systems, providing a stepping stone toward full cryoscope-based calibration.

title: Diffusivity In Dissipative Quantum Transport From An Exactly Solvable Krylov Chain
authors: Jorge Noronha Zhi-Li Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The computation of transport coefficients in interacting quantum many-body systems is rarely analytically accessible. Here, we develop a new Krylov-space mechanism that makes the leading density dependent correction to Green-Kubo diffusivity calculable in the strong-dissipation regime of a one-dimensional noisy spin-[MATH] XXZ chain. This is done by showing that the density-polarization-dressed bond coherence generates a Krylov subspace where repeated action of the dissipator closes exactly on an explicitly identifiable operator family. Within this subspace, the dissipative dynamics is then mapped onto a self-similar semi-infinite chain with a boundary defect. Surprisingly, Lanczos coefficients of the Krylov chain and its boundary Green's function can be determined exactly. The latter then determines the exact leading density-dependent correction to the diffusivity. Finally, we calculate analytically the full boundary-to-bulk Green's function and find that it decays exponentially along the emergent Krylov chain.
tldr: The paper introduces an exactly solvable Krylov-space framework to compute the leading density-dependent correction to Green-Kubo diffusivity in a strongly dissipative one-dimensional noisy XXZ spin chain.
motivation: Transport coefficients in interacting quantum many-body systems are rarely analytically accessible, especially in the strong-dissipation regime where standard perturbative or numerical methods become challenging.
method: The authors identify a Krylov subspace generated by density-polarization-dressed bond coherence in which the dissipator closes on an explicitly known operator family, mapping the dissipative dynamics onto a semi-infinite chain with a boundary defect. title: Large-scale Quantum Simulations Of Dissipative Spin-1/2 Heisenberg Chains
authors: Jo\~ao C. Getelina, Andrew Cox, Muhammad Asaduzzaman, Omar Alsheikh, Ryan S. Bennink, James K. Freericks, Alexander F. Kemper
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum many-body system coupled to an environment relaxes to a nonequilibrium steady state that can sustain order with no equilibrium counterpart. Computing such steady states is harder than closed-system dynamics as the density matrix problem squares the Hilbert-space dimension, and no free energy selects the steady state. The dissipative spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain is a benchmark example for nonequilibrium steady state physics; various methods have each calculated its phase diagram but do not agree, and a controlled determination at large system size has remained out of reach. Here we simulate the Lindblad dynamics of chains of up to 50 sites on the superconducting processor ibm_kingston -- 100 simultaneously active qubits at up to 1700 entangling-gate depths -- realizing the dissipation via Stinespring dilation. The system's dissipative evolution is a self-correcting mechanism that effectively erases errors, so hardware noise enters only as a weak competing dissipator. We measure static structure factors and resolve ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, spin-density-wave, and paramagnetic steady states, mapping the phase diagram with 117 quantum hardware data points across the [MATH]--[MATH] plane. We uncover a rich non-equilibrium phase diagram of ordered phases with only remnants of the mean-field order, and where sharp transitions give way to the crossovers expected in one dimension. We also find the existence of an incipient (Trotter-induced) spin density wave phase, highlighting the potential of controlled Trotterization as a tool to engineer various magnetic phases in dissipative spin systems. Our quantum simulations largely settle the lingering uncertainty regarding the correct phase diagram of this benchmark system. Moreover, they show that quantum computers are now a feasible tool for addressing scientific questions involving dissipative quantum systems.
tldr: The paper simulates Lindblad dynamics of dissipative spin-1/2 Heisenberg chains up to 50 sites on a superconducting quantum processor, mapping the nonequilibrium phase diagram.
motivation: Computing nonequilibrium steady states of open quantum many-body systems is challenging, and existing methods disagree on the phase diagram of the benchmark dissipative Heisenberg chain.
method: They use Stinespring dilation to realize dissipation on ibm_kingston with up to 100 qubits and 1700 entangling-gate depths, measuring static structure factors across a parameter plane.
result: They resolve ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, spin-density-wave, and paramagnetic steady states, uncovering non-equilibrium ordered phases, crossovers, and an incipient Trotter-induced spin density wave.
conclusion: The quantum simulations largely settle the phase diagram of this benchmark system and demonstrate that quantum computers are feasible for studying dissipative quantum systems.

title: Partial Projected Ensembles Reveal Slow Tilt-constrained Information Spreading
authors: Yi-Rui Zhang, Yu-Jun Zhao, Han-Ze Li, Jian-Xin Zhong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Projected ensembles reveal information about quantum many-body dynamics beyond the reduced density matrix. Here we investigate how spatial constraints affect the emergence of this information in a kicked Ising chain with a spatially varying longitudinal field. We consider partial projected ensembles, obtained by measuring a remote region while leaving an intervening buffer unobserved. Our numerical results reveal a pronounced contrast between nearly ballistic correlation onset in the ergodic regime and strongly delayed onset in the tilt-constrained regime, corroborated by quantum mutual information. Despite these different onset scales, the conditional-state fluctuations decrease approximately exponentially with buffer length in both regimes. Full projected ensembles additionally exhibit slow relaxation and persistent measurement-basis dependence in their higher moments. We establish an information-theoretic characterization of the connected second moment and use a solvable dephasing model with effective-basis measurements to illustrate the separation of phase accumulation and coherence loss. Within this model, a factorially suppressed coupling envelope yields sublogarithmic spreading consistent with the finite-distance onset trends. Our results identify partial projected ensembles as probes of the distinction between the time required for correlations to develop and the information that remains accessible under partial observation.

motivation: Understanding how spatial constraints affect the emergence and accessibility of information in quantum many-body dynamics beyond the reduced density matrix.
method: Numerically simulate partial projected ensembles in a kicked Ising chain with a spatially varying longitudinal field by measuring a remote region while leaving an intervening buffer unobserved, and analyze conditional-state fluctuations, quantum mutual information, and a solvable dephasing model with effective-basis measurements.
result: The ergodic regime exhibits nearly ballistic correlation onset, whereas the tilt-constrained regime shows strongly delayed onset; conditional-state fluctuations decay approximately exponentially with buffer length, and full projected ensembles display slow relaxation and persistent measurement-basis dependence in higher moments.
conclusion: Partial projected ensembles provide a probe that distinguishes the time required for correlations to develop from the information that remains accessible under partial observation, with an information-theoretic characterization of the connected second moment.

title: Floquet Dressing And Bath Spectral Effects On The Geometric Phase Of A Driven Dissipative Qubit
authors: Chirag Arora
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16609v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building on recent work by Wang et al. on the dissipative geometric phase (GP) in the spin-boson model (SBM), the GP dynamics of a periodically driven symmetric SBM are investigated using the numerically exact process-tensor time-evolving matrix product operator (PT-TEMPO) method. A symmetric two-level system subjected to a longitudinal monochromatic drive along the same system coordinate that couples to an Ohmic bosonic environment exhibits rich GP dynamics arising from the interplay between driving and dissipation. To isolate cooperative drive-bath effects, a non-additive GP contribution is introduced that separates the driven dissipative response from its driven-unitary and undriven-dissipative components. Periodic driving is found to either suppress or enhance bath-induced GP deformation depending on the interplay between drive and bath timescales. These trends are interpreted through Floquet spectral steering, whereby the drive redistributes the coherent dynamics among quasienergy sidebands whose transition frequencies and Fourier-resolved system-bath matrix elements determine their coupling to the environmental spectrum. Floquet analysis shows that the dominant dissipative pathways are governed jointly by Floquet matrix-element weights and bath spectral overlap, rather than by either alone. These results connect Floquet engineering, quantum dissipation, and GP dynamics and establish periodic driving as a means of controlling the GP of open quantum systems (OQSs).

motivation: Building on recent work on dissipative geometric phases in the spin-boson model, the authors aim to understand the interplay between Floquet driving and dissipation in open quantum systems.
method: A symmetric two-level system coupled to an Ohmic bosonic bath and subjected to a longitudinal monochromatic drive is simulated with the numerically exact process-tensor time-evolving matrix product operator (PT-TEMPO) method, supplemented by Floquet analysis to identify dominant dissipative pathways.
result: Periodic driving can either suppress or enhance bath-induced geometric phase deformation depending on the drive-bath timescale interplay, and the dominant dissipative pathways are jointly determined by Floquet matrix-element weights and bath spectral overlap.
conclusion: The results connect Floquet engineering, quantum dissipation, and geometric phase dynamics, establishing periodic driving as a tool to control geometric phases in open quantum systems.

title: Pretty Good Quantum State Transfer Via Transcendental Edge Weights
authors: Addison Ballif, Mark Kempton, James B. Larsen, Kellon Sandall, Christino Tamon, Trevor Wai
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16549v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that if we take a rooted product of a circulant graph with universal perfect state transfer with a path of fixed length whose end edge is weighted with a transcendental number, then there is pretty good state transfer between any pair of endpoints of these paths. As a consequence, in a path with an even number of vertices with transcendental weights on the two edges incident to the endpoints, there is pretty good state transfer.
tldr: The authors prove that rooted products of circulant graphs having universal perfect state transfer with a fixed-length path, where the end edge is weighted by a transcendental number, exhibit pretty good state transfer between the path endpoints.
motivation: Perfect state transfer in continuous-time quantum walks on spin networks is rare, so identifying graph constructions that guarantee near-perfect (pretty good) transfer is valuable for understanding when reliable state transfer is achievable.
method: The work uses spectral graph theory and algebraic number theory arguments, exploiting the transcendental nature of the edge weight to control eigenvalue ratios and avoid the rational-commensurability obstructions that block exact perfect state transfer.
result: They show pretty good state transfer between any pair of path endpoints in such rooted products, and as a corollary obtain pretty good state transfer in even-vertex paths with transcendental weights on the two edges incident to the endpoints.
conclusion: Transcendental edge weights provide a robust design principle for constructing graphs with pretty good state transfer, extending known results on perfect state transfer in circulant-based network structures.

title: Link-middle-cut Lower Bounds For Clifford Circuit Synthesis
authors: S{\o}ren Fuglede J{\o}rgensen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minimizing the number of CNOT gates required to synthesize a Clifford operator is a central problem in quantum circuit optimization. We extend the link--middle--cut (LMC) framework for linear reversible circuits to Clifford operators represented by binary symplectic tableaux. By introducing block-support connectivity graphs and determinantal invariants, we obtain efficiently computable lower bounds on ancilla-free CNOT complexity. We prove that these bounds are tight for qubit permutations: a permutation of [MATH] qubits with [MATH] cycles requires exactly [MATH] CNOT gates, even when arbitrary one-qubit Clifford gates are available. We also derive efficiently computable bounds for synthesis up to a permutation of the output qubits, corresponding to free qubit relabeling. Finally, we further demonstrate the utility of the bound by using it as an admissible heuristic for [MATH]-based Clifford synthesis and show that, on benchmark instances, the resulting search can prove optimality beyond what was possible with earlier SAT-based methods, and that it may be used in combination with earlier [MATH] heuristics to improve the CNOT counts obtained through heuristic search.
tldr: The paper extends the link-middle-cut framework to derive efficiently computable lower bounds on CNOT gate counts for synthesizing Clifford operators, with tight bounds for qubit permutations.
motivation: Minimizing CNOT gates in Clifford circuits is central to quantum circuit optimization, but efficient lower bounds for ancilla-free synthesis were lacking.
method: The authors generalize the link-middle-cut framework using binary symplectic tableaux, block-support connectivity graphs, and determinantal invariants to compute lower bounds.
result: They prove tight bounds for qubit permutations (n-c CNOTs for c cycles), derive bounds up to output qubit permutation, and use them as admissible heuristics for A*-based synthesis, outperforming SAT-based methods.
conclusion: The proposed lower bounds provide a practical tool for optimal Clifford synthesis and can improve heuristic search CNOT counts.

title: Parity-Sensitive Fourier Uncertainty And Zero-Set Rigidity On The Finite Parabola
authors: Dongwei Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be prime, let [MATH] satisfy [MATH], and set \[ F(a,b)=\sum_{x\in R}c_x\omega^{ax^2+bx}, \qquad (a,b)\in\mathbb F_p^2, \qquad c_x\ne0, \] where [MATH]. We prove a parity-sensitive uncertainty principle for complex Fourier spectra supported on the finite parabola. If [MATH], then \[ |Z(F)|\le p+2r-2, \] and the bound is sharp for every even support size [MATH], including the endpoint [MATH]. If [MATH], then \[ |Z(F)|\le \min\{p+2r-2,\,r(r+1)\}. \] Thus fixed odd spectral sparsity forces a number of zeros bounded independently of [MATH], whereas sufficiently large even zero sets are rigid: for even support [MATH], if [MATH], then [MATH] vanishes identically on a nonvertical affine line and has at most [MATH] further zeros. The proof reduces arbitrary complex coefficients to cyclotomic data and uses a truncated [MATH]-adic expansion. The first nonzero finite-field jets satisfy \[ \partial_b^2Q_j=\partial_aQ_{j-1}, \] turning the two-dimensional zero problem into a multiplicity and component-persistence problem for algebraic curves. As an application, we solve the total-support uncertainty problem for the standard complete set of [MATH] mutually unbiased bases in [MATH]: \[ \min_{0\ne\psi\in\mathbb C^p} \sum_j |_{\mathcal B_j}(\psi)| =p^2-p+2. \] We also classify all extremizing projective states and give an exact enumeration formula.
