motivation: To establish sharp uncertainty principles and rigidity constraints for finite-field Fourier transforms supported on a parabola, and to resolve a total-support uncertainty problem for mutually unbiased bases.
method: Reduces arbitrary complex coefficients to cyclotomic data using a truncated p-adic expansion and analyzes finite-field jets to turn the zero problem into a multiplicity and component-persistence problem for algebraic curves.
result: When the spectral support is odd, the zero set satisfies |Z(F)| ≤ p+2r−2, sharp for every even support size; for large even zero sets, F vanishes on a nonvertical affine line and has at most r(r+1) further zeros; for MUBs, the minimum total support is p^2−p+2 with a classification of extremizers.
conclusion: The paper provides sharp uncertainty and rigidity bounds for finite parabolic Fourier spectra and gives an exact enumeration formula for the MUB total-support uncertainty problem.

title: Qdmag: A Python Package For Simulating Nonequilibrium Magnetization Of Molecules Using Quantum Master Equations
authors: Shuanglong Liu, Xiao Chen, Andrew Cupo, James N. Fry, Hai-Ping Cheng
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present qdmag, a computational utility for calculating the magnetization of magnetic molecules in a time-varying external magnetic field by solving a generalized Lindblad quantum master equation with spin-phonon coupling treated as a dissipation term. The package relies on the spin Hamiltonian formalism, which includes both the magnetic exchange interactions and the zero-field splitting (ZFS) interaction. Different types of magnetic exchange interaction and ZFS terms up to 12th order, which are written in terms of the extended Stevens operators, are supported. qdmag enables long-time evolution of magnetization for up to a few milliseconds, which is achieved through a staircase approximation of the magnetic field as a function of time. For high-dimensional spin Hamiltonians, a lower-dimensional effective Hamiltonian is constructed to make the calculations computationally feasible. Three case studies of one-spin, two-spin, and three-spin systems are presented to demonstrate the usage of qdmag. Our work offers a computational tool to bridge the gap between theoretical development and numerical calculations of spin dynamics in the presence of spin-phonon coupling.
tldr: qdmag is a Python package that simulates nonequilibrium magnetization of magnetic molecules by solving a generalized Lindblad quantum master equation with spin-phonon coupling.
motivation: To bridge theoretical spin dynamics and numerical calculations, providing a computational tool for magnetization in time-varying magnetic fields.
method: Uses a spin Hamiltonian with magnetic exchange and zero-field splitting up to 12th order, a Lindblad master equation with spin-phonon dissipation, a staircase approximation for long-time evolution, and an effective Hamiltonian reduction for high-dimensional systems.
result: Demonstrates the package on one-, two-, and three-spin systems, enabling magnetization simulations up to a few milliseconds.
conclusion: qdmag offers a practical computational utility for studying nonequilibrium spin dynamics in magnetic molecules with spin-phonon coupling.

title: Truncated Hybrid Tensor Networks For Distributed Quantum Simulation
authors: Yong Liu, Guangyao Huang, Weixu Shi, Yizhi Wang, Jiandong Ouyang, Zeqian Chen, Junjie Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulation of quantum many-body systems is a principal application of quantum computing, but available devices remain limited by the number of qubits and cannot accommodate systems of the desired size. One approach is to host a large evolution across several modest distributed systems that exchange classical information alone. Current protocols such as circuit knitting incur a quasi-probability sampling cost that grows exponentially with the number of remote gates across the cut, even when physical correlations across the cut are actually bounded. In this work, we present a truncated hybrid tensor network (THTN) framework in which a remote two-body gate is applied as a sum of local unitaries on the subsystems, linked by a classical connecting tensor, and an interface truncation retains Schmidt modes across the cut. Remote gates between the same subsystems can be merged on one connector, so non-one-dimensional models, such as layered partitions with strong intra-layer and weaker interlayer couplings, may be cast onto a one-dimensional cut. The retained non-negative Schmidt coefficients also define a sampling rule for local observables. We validate this distributed protocol by classical simulation against time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) at the same bond dimension. The truncated dynamics track the TEBD references on chains and ladders, with the clearest gain on a layered model.
tldr: A truncated hybrid tensor network framework for distributed quantum simulation that reduces the sampling cost of remote gates by retaining Schmidt modes across the cut.
motivation: Simulating large quantum many-body systems on limited quantum devices requires distributing the computation, but existing circuit knitting methods incur exponential sampling overhead with the number of remote gates, even when cross-cut correlations are bounded.
method: Remote two-body gates are applied as sums of local unitaries linked by a classical connecting tensor, with interface truncation retaining non-negative Schmidt coefficients; remote gates between the same subsystems can be merged onto one connector, and the retained coefficients define a sampling rule for local observables.
result: Classical simulation against time-evolving block decimation at the same bond dimension shows that the truncated dynamics track the references on chains and ladders, with the clearest gain on a layered model.
conclusion: The truncated hybrid tensor network approach enables efficient distributed quantum simulation when physical correlations across the cut are bounded, and can cast non-one-dimensional partitions onto a one-dimensional cut.

title: Cpm-ldpc Codes Attaining The Minimum-Distance Bound
authors: Kenta Kasai
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study binary quasi-cyclic LDPC codes whose parity-check matrices are full arrays of single circulant permutation matrices (CPMs), referred to here as CPM-LDPC codes. Their minimum distance is at most [MATH], where [MATH] is the column weight. For every fixed pair of column and row weights [MATH], we show that this bound is attained for all sufficiently large integer lift sizes. First, we give one integer exponent matrix independent of the lift size [MATH]. Second, we show that independent uniform exponent choices attain the bound with probability [MATH]. Both proofs use cycle conditions required by low-weight codewords and a lower bound on the number of terms in vectors satisfying polynomial check equations. Neither construction requires [MATH] to be prime. We also give small-lift arrays attaining the bound 24 for [MATH], [MATH], and arrays with distance at least 28 for [MATH], [MATH], together with computational distance verification.
tldr: The paper constructs binary quasi-cyclic CPM-LDPC codes that attain the minimum-distance bound for sufficiently large lift sizes.
motivation: LDPC codes with large minimum distance are desirable for reliable communication, and quasi-cyclic constructions are practical and structurally appealing.
method: The proofs use cycle conditions for low-weight codewords and a lower bound on the number of terms in vectors satisfying polynomial check equations, giving both a deterministic exponent matrix and a probabilistic independent uniform exponent choice.
result: The minimum-distance bound is attained for all sufficiently large lift sizes without requiring the lift size to be prime; small-lift arrays attaining distance 24 and at least 28 are also provided with computational verification.
conclusion: The work establishes constructions of CPM-LDPC codes that meet the minimum-distance bound, advancing classical coding theory but without direct quantum information implications.

title: List Decoding, Linear Hashing, And Furstenberg Over $\mathbb{F}_q$
authors: Geoffrey Mon Vinayak M. Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give new bounds for list sizes of random linear codes at capacity, max loads of linear hash functions, and Furstenberg sets, over every finite field [MATH]. 1. Random linear codes over [MATH] with rate [MATH] are [MATH]-list decodable with high probability for all values of [MATH], including the high error regime. This nearly matches the list size lower bound of [MATH] due to Guruswami, Li, Mosheiff, Resch, Silas, and Wootters [IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 2022]. Our bound is the first uniform improvement for [MATH] since Guruswami, H{\aa}stad, and Kopparty [STOC 2010]. 2. Linear hash functions over [MATH] hashing [MATH] balls to [MATH] bins achieve maximum load [MATH], both in expectation and with probability [MATH]. This nearly matches the lower bound of [MATH]. Previously, only a polylogarithmic upper bound was known for [MATH], due to Alon, Dietzfelbinger, Miltersen, Petrank, and Tardos [J. ACM 1999]. We reduce list decodability and linear hashing to strong Furstenberg set lower bounds, which we prove using a new polynomial method of multiplicity gaps. While previous polynomial methods analyze a set [MATH] by studying polynomials that vanish on it, we consider polynomials that vanish everywhere, but with higher multiplicity inside [MATH] than outside.
tldr: The paper gives new bounds on list sizes of random linear codes, maximum loads of linear hash functions, and Furstenberg sets over finite fields using a new polynomial method of multiplicity gaps.
motivation: Prior list-decoding bounds for random linear codes had not seen a uniform improvement since 2010, and linear hashing only had polylogarithmic upper bounds for maximum load in some regimes.
method: The authors reduce list decodability and linear hashing to strong Furstenberg set lower bounds, which they prove using a polynomial method that considers polynomials vanishing everywhere but with higher multiplicity inside a set than outside it.
result: Random linear codes over F_q with rate approaching capacity are list-decodable with high probability for all error regimes, nearly matching known lower bounds; linear hash functions achieve maximum load nearly matching the lower bound, improving prior upper bounds.
conclusion: The work provides the first uniform improvement in list decoding bounds for random linear codes since 2010 and demonstrates the power of the multiplicity-gap polynomial method for these combinatorial problems.

title: Towards Surrogate Based Dequantization Of Quantum Reinforcement Learning
authors: Pablo Rodriguez-Grasa, Sofiene Jerbi, Mikel Sanz, Ryan Sweke
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, the utility of parameterized quantum circuits as function approximators has been widely studied. In the context of reinforcement learning, this approach has led to variational quantum algorithms such as quantum Q-learning. While these methods show promising empirical results, and can provide provable advantages for artificial problems, it remains unclear whether they can provide a provable quantum advantage over classical approaches for problems of practical relevance. A natural way to investigate this question is through the lens of dequantization: The construction of efficient classical algorithms capable of matching the performance of quantum variational methods. Building on recent kernel-based dequantization results for supervised learning, we take steps towards extending this surrogate-based dequantization program to reinforcement learning. Specifically, we study the simplified setting of reinforcement learning with a uniform generative model in which uniformly random state-action samples are available, which models the regime of sampling from a large experience replay buffer after sufficient exploration. Within this setting, we provide finite sample guarantees for classical kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration, with classical kernels designed to match the inductive bias of particular parameterized quantum circuits. Using these results, we then provide a set of sufficient conditions, on the data-encoding strategy of a parameterized quantum circuit, the corresponding classical kernel, and the problem structure, under which kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration provides a meaningful dequantization of quantum Q-learning, in this simplified setting. Apart from providing rigorous dequantization guarantees when these conditions are met, these results also motivate the use of kernelized fitted Q-iteration as a dequantization heuristic when these sufficient conditions cannot be verified.
tldr: The paper develops classical kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration to dequantize quantum Q-learning in a simplified uniform generative model, providing finite-sample guarantees and sufficient conditions for meaningful dequantization.
motivation: Quantum reinforcement learning with parameterized quantum circuits shows empirical promise, but it remains unclear whether it offers provable quantum advantage over classical approaches for practical problems.
method: Extends kernel-based dequantization from supervised learning to reinforcement learning by using classical kernels designed to match the inductive bias of parameterized quantum circuits, and analyzes kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration with uniformly random state-action samples.
result: Provides finite-sample guarantees and sufficient conditions on data-encoding strategy, classical kernel, and problem structure under which kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration matches quantum Q-learning in the simplified setting.
conclusion: The work takes steps toward dequantizing quantum reinforcement learning and motivates kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration as a dequantization heuristic when sufficient conditions cannot be verified.

title: Adaptive Detection Of Rabi Signals Under Composite Hypotheses
authors: So Chigusa
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by searches for weak coherent drives, we formulate repeated quantum sensing with a fixed shot budget as an asymmetric composite hypothesis test. Taking Rabi sensing as a concrete example, we benchmark detection power, sensitivity, and Type-II error exponents in the resonant case with unknown signal amplitude and phase. We compare non-adaptive population and transverse readouts with a myopic Bayesian policy that selects each projective axis by maximizing the expected information gain in one step. The common decision statistic is a log Bayes factor, with a policy specific threshold calibrated under the null to enforce a common Type-I error. A weak signal expansion shows that population readout is phase independent but quadratic in amplitude, giving [MATH] sensitivity, whereas transverse readout is linear in amplitude and permits [MATH] sensitivity without adaptation, but is phase-dependent. In Monte Carlo pseudoexperiments, the adaptive policy exploits posterior information about the unknown direction to guide subsequent readouts; its sensitivity is consistent with [MATH] over the simulated large [MATH] range and, at the largest simulated shot counts, outperforms the fixed transverse schedules. Its phase-averaged effective Type-II exponent also exceeds the non-adaptive references over the simulated range. These results demonstrate the finite budget value of exploiting nuisance parameter information under calibrated false positive control.
tldr: This paper formulates repeated quantum sensing of weak coherent drives as an asymmetric composite hypothesis test and compares adaptive Bayesian policies against non-adaptive readouts for Rabi signal detection.
motivation: Motivated by searches for weak coherent drives, the author aims to improve detection power and sensitivity under a fixed shot budget when signal amplitude and phase are unknown.
method: The detection problem is cast as a composite hypothesis test, benchmarking non-adaptive population and transverse readouts against a myopic Bayesian policy that selects projective axes to maximize expected information gain. A weak-signal expansion and Monte Carlo pseudoexperiments are used to compare sensitivity and Type-II error exponents.
result: Population readout is phase-independent but quadratic in amplitude, while transverse readout is linear but phase-dependent. The adaptive policy exploits posterior information to guide subsequent measurements, achieving sensitivity consistent with 1/M scaling and outperforming fixed transverse schedules at large shot counts.
conclusion: The adaptive strategy demonstrates finite-budget value of exploiting nuisance parameter information under calibrated false-positive control, advancing practical quantum sensing protocols.

title: Hadamard Rigidity And Sharp Stability In The Completely Bounded Bohnenblust--Hille Inequality
authors: Daniel N\'u\~nez-Alarc\'on, Daniel M. Pellegrino, Eduardo V. Teixeira
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The completely bounded Bohnenblust--Hille inequality of Arunachalam, Dutt, Escudero Guti\'errez and Palazuelos controls coefficient summability with optimal constant one, independently of the ambient dimension. We classify all nonzero equality cases over both the real and complex fields: they are precisely scalar multiples of Hadamard chains supported on equal-sided Cartesian boxes. Thus equality determines both the support and the factorization of the coefficient tensor. For each fixed degree [MATH], we also establish sharp structural stability. A form with completely bounded norm one and deficit [MATH] lies within [MATH], in the critical coefficient [MATH] norm, of both a flat unimodular path and a normalized unitary chain on the same box. The corresponding unimodular and scaled unitary edges satisfy a matching normalized Frobenius estimate. At zero deficit both approximants coincide with the original Hadamard chain. All constants are independent of the ambient dimension, and the exponent [MATH] is optimal for both approximations over either field.
tldr: The paper fully classifies the equality cases of the completely bounded Bohnenblust–Hille inequality and proves dimension-independent sharp stability estimates for near-equality forms.
motivation: The completely bounded Bohnenblust–Hille inequality, formulated in the operator-space setting by Arunachalam, Dutt, Escudero Gutiérrez and Palazuelos, controls coefficient summability with optimal constant independent of dimension, but its extremal and near-extremal structure was previously unknown.
method: The authors analyze equality conditions over both real and complex fields using operator-space and tensor-product techniques, showing extremal forms are scalar multiples of Hadamard chains on equal-sided Cartesian boxes, and then derive quantitative stability bounds in the critical coefficient norm and normalized Frobenius norm.
result: Equality holds precisely for Hadamard chains supported on equal-sided Cartesian boxes, and any form of completely bounded norm one with small deficit lies within a dimension-independent distance of a flat unimodular path and a normalized unitary chain, with the exponent shown to be optimal over either field.
conclusion: The work provides a rigid structural characterization and sharp, dimension-free stability for the completely bounded Bohnenblust–Hille inequality, extending the analytic theory underlying certain quantum-information-inspired inequalities.

title: Amortized Relaxed Locally Decodable Codes
authors: Justin Zhang Jeremiah Blocki
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Locally decodable codes (LDCs) enable recovery of any message symbol by probing only a small number of positions in a possibly corrupted codeword. The central parameters of an LDC are its rate, locality, and error tolerance. Ideally, one would like all three parameters to be constant. However, classical lower bounds show that such codes cannot exist. A recent line of work introduced amortized locally decodable codes (aLDCs), in which the decoder is tasked with recovering an entire block of consecutive message symbols rather than a single symbol. While prior work obtained ideal aLDCs with constant rate, constant error tolerance, and constant amortized locality, those constructions relied on either shared randomness hidden from the channel or computational assumptions restricting the channel. Another well-studied relaxation is the notion of a relaxed locally decodable code (RLDC), in which the decoder may output a special failure symbol [MATH] rather than risk decoding incorrectly. In this work, we introduce the notion of an amortized relaxed locally decodable code (aRLDC), combining amortized decoding with the relaxed decoding paradigm. Unlike prior ideal aLDC constructions, our model is fully information-theoretic and makes no assumptions about shared randomness or computational limitations of the adversarial channel. We construct the first aRLDC with constant rate, constant error tolerance, and constant amortized locality. Moreover, for any block of length [MATH], our decoder achieves amortized locality [MATH], where [MATH] is the error tolerance parameter. Thus, asymptotically, recovering a long block requires essentially less than two codeword probe per message symbol recovered. By contrast, without amortization no RLDC can simultaneously achieve constant rate, constant error tolerance, and constant locality.
tldr: The paper introduces amortized relaxed locally decodable codes (aRLDCs) and constructs the first such codes with constant rate and constant relative distance.

title: Linear Programming Bounds For Locally Recovery Codes Ii
authors: Maosheng Xiong Ming-Hsuan Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16044v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a polynomial-size linear programming bound for [MATH]-ary all-symbol locally recoverable codes with locality parameters [MATH], without assuming linearity. The key idea is to keep, for every ordered pair of codewords and every selected recovery view, the joint Hamming weight on the helper set, the recovered coordinate, and the rest of the code -- rather than collapsing this triple into a single distance, as earlier formulations do. Averaging this three-block distribution over recovery views of the same length yields exact identities linking it to the global distance distribution, together with nonnegative product-Krawtchouk constraints that encode locality and spectral positivity simultaneously. The resulting LP has polynomially many variables, its optimum dominates the ordinary Delsarte bound, and an earlier outside-distance formulation, the convex-hull bound of Li--Wei--Xiong, and the dual-based bound of Gruica--Jany--Ravagnani all arise from it as coarser marginals. Exact rational certificates over [MATH] show the bound is strictly stronger than the best of these prior LPs in thirteen of fifteen tested cases, pinning down seven exact maximum code sizes and twelve exact maximum linear dimensions.
tldr: The paper presents a polynomial-size linear programming bound for classical locally recoverable codes using a three-block joint Hamming weight distribution.
motivation: Locally recoverable codes are important for distributed storage, and existing bounds on their maximum size are often weaker or less general than desired.
method: It keeps the joint Hamming weight on the helper set, the recovered coordinate, and the rest of the code for each ordered pair of codewords and recovery view, then averages over views to derive exact identities and nonnegative product-Krawtchouk constraints.
result: The resulting LP dominates the ordinary Delsarte bound and prior bounds, yielding strictly stronger bounds in 13 of 15 tested cases and pinning down exact maximum code sizes and linear dimensions.
conclusion: This provides a unified and stronger LP framework for bounding locally recoverable codes, with prior formulations arising as coarser marginals.

title: Two Variants Of Twisted Reed-Solomon Codes
authors: Haojie Gu, Huiyue Lei, Jun Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalized Reed-Solomon codes and twisted generalized Reed-Solomon codes provide important sources of maximum distance separable codes. In this paper, we study two variants obtained by introducing column twists and simultaneous row-column twists into Reed-Solomon-type evaluation codes. For the column-twisted family, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the code to be MDS in terms of explicit subset product conditions. Under the stated parameter assumptions, the Schur square has dimension 2k+1, which leads to MDS codes that are not equivalent to Reed-Solomon codes. For the row-column twisted family, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the MDS property in terms of elementary symmetric functions. The larger Schur-square dimension provides a further distinction from both Reed-Solomon codes and known twisted families, thereby yielding new non-RS MDS codes. Finally, explicit parity-check matrices and dual descriptions are obtained for both code families. These results provide a foundation for subsequent studies of self-orthogonality, hull dimensions, and applications to quantum-code constructions.
tldr: The paper introduces two variants of twisted Reed-Solomon codes and derives MDS conditions via subset products and elementary symmetric functions, with potential applications to quantum-code constructions.
motivation: To enlarge the family of MDS codes beyond Reed-Solomon and known twisted codes, providing new non-RS MDS codes and tools for quantum code design.
method: Column twists and simultaneous row-column twists are applied to Reed-Solomon evaluation codes; necessary and sufficient MDS conditions are obtained using subset product and elementary symmetric functions, along with Schur square dimension analysis and parity-check/dual descriptions.
result: The column-twisted family has Schur square dimension 2k+1 and yields new non-RS MDS codes; the row-column twisted family has larger Schur-square dimension and distinct MDS conditions.
conclusion: These code families provide a foundation for subsequent studies of self-orthogonality, hull dimensions, and applications to quantum-code constructions.

title: On Sequence Reconstruction Problem For Q-ary Deletion Channels
authors: Xiang Wang, Han Li, Fang-Wei Fu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The sequence reconstruction problem for [MATH]-ary deletion channels, introduced by Levenshtein in 2001, concerns the minimum number of channels required to uniquely recover a transmitted sequence when each channel introduces exactly [MATH] deletions. Combinatorially, it is equivalent to determining [MATH], the maximum intersection size of two [MATH]-deletion balls with centers at Levenshtein distance at least [MATH], for [MATH]-ary sequences of length [MATH] over the alphabet \(\Sigma_q=\{0,1,\dots,q-1\}\). Levenshtein solved the uncoded case [MATH] for all [MATH]; subsequently, Gabrys and Yaakobi determined [MATH], and Wang et al. extended the result to [MATH]. In this paper, we study the problem for \(q\)-ary sequences under minimum Levenshtein distance \(d=2\) with channels that introduce exactly \(t\) deletions. We determine the exact value of \(N_q(n,2,t)\) for all \(t\ge 2, q\geq 4\), and for sufficiently large \(n\), and construct explicit pairs of sequences attaining the maximum intersection. Furthermore, for each [MATH], we characterize all extremal sequence pairs. In particular, if the intersection size matches the first two terms of \(N_q(n,2,t)\), then the two center sequences must contain, at the same positions, length-5 blocks of the forms \((a,b,c,a,b)\) and \((b,a,c,b,a)\) for some distinct \(a,b,c\in\Sigma_q\); for \(t\ge q+2\), the exact maximum \(N_q(n,2,t)\) is attained precisely by \(2q!\) unordered pairs of sequences with a specific block structure. Asymptotically, we prove that for \(q\ge 4\) and \(t\ge 2\), \[ N_q(n,2,t)={(t-2)!}n^{t-2}-{(t-3)!}n^{t-3}+{4(t-4)!}n^{t-4}+O(n^{t-5}). \] Moreover, \(N_q(n,2,t)\) and \(N_{q-1}(n,2,t)\) share their first \(q-1\) terms, and for \(t\ge q\) the coefficient of \(n^{t-q}\) in their difference is \({(t-q)!}\).
tldr: The paper determines the exact maximum intersection size of q-ary deletion balls for centers at Levenshtein distance 2, solving the sequence reconstruction problem for deletion channels with q≥4 and large n.
motivation: Sequence reconstruction for deletion channels asks how many noisy copies are needed to uniquely recover a transmitted sequence; this reduces to computing the maximum intersection of deletion balls.
method: Using combinatorial analysis and explicit constructions of extremal sequence pairs, the authors derive exact values for N_q(n,2,t) and characterize all extremal pairs.
result: For q≥4, t≥2, and sufficiently large n, N_q(n,2,t) = (t-2)! n^{t-2} - (t-3)! n^{t-3} + 4(t-4)! n^{t-4} + O(n^{t-5}), with explicit block structures attaining the maximum.
conclusion: The results extend previous work on deletion channel sequence reconstruction to q-ary alphabets and provide a complete characterization of extremal configurations.

title: Further Results On Binary Codes Of Covering Radius 2 And Saturating Sets In Projective Spaces
authors: Alexander A. Davydov, Stefano Marcugini, Fernanda Pambianco, Stephen Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16078v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The length function [MATH] is the smallest length of a binary linear code with codimension (redundancy) [MATH] and covering radius [MATH]. Let [MATH] be the smallest size of a [MATH]-saturating set in the projective space [MATH]. It is known that [MATH]. We obtain the following new upper bounds on [MATH], which yield a decrease [MATH] compared to the best previously known upper bounds: [MATH] and [MATH]. To obtain these bounds, we construct a new infinite code family, using distinct versions of the [MATH]-concatenating constructions of covering codes; some of these versions are proposed in this paper. We also obtain new useful partitions of column sets of parity check matrices of some codes. The asymptotic covering density [MATH], provided by the codes of the new family, is smaller than previously known one and gives rise to the new upper bound [MATH] on the constant [MATH] of the Green's Open Problem 40.

motivation: The length function and saturating sets are central objects in classical coding theory, and tightening known upper bounds (including Green's Open Problem 40) has been an open challenge.
method: The authors use new versions of q-concatenating constructions of covering codes to build an infinite code family, and they obtain new partitions of column sets of parity-check matrices.
result: New upper bounds on the length function are obtained, giving a decrease relative to the best previously known bounds, along with an improved asymptotic covering density and a new bound on the constant of Green's Open Problem 40.
conclusion: The work advances classical covering-code theory and projective-geometry combinatorics, but it has no quantum information, thermodynamic, networking, or hybrid-platform content.

title: On Twisted Roth-Lempel Codes
authors: Huiyue Lei, Haojie Gu, Jun Zhang, Haiyan Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 1989, Roth and Lempel constructed a well-known family of non-Reed-Solomon maximum distance separable (MDS) codes. For decades, this family of codes has attracted extensive research attention due to its algebraic structure, low-complexity decoding, and broad applications in cryptography and data storage. In this paper, we present a class of twisted Roth-Lempel codes. We investigate their minimum distance, MDS and NMDS properties. Specifically, we determine the necessary and sufficient conditions for the TRL codes to have minimum distance n-k or n-k+1. Furthermore, we determine the necessary and sufficient conditions for the TRL code to be an MDS or NMDS code. Moreover, we show that the dimension of the Schur square of the TRL code is at least 2k+1, and thus the TRL code is a non-RS code inequivalent to the corresponding RL code.
tldr: The paper introduces twisted Roth-Lempel (TRL) codes and derives necessary and sufficient conditions for their minimum distance, MDS/NMDS properties, and shows their Schur square dimension is at least 2k+1, proving they are non-Reed-Solomon codes inequivalent to the corresponding Roth-Lempel codes.
motivation: Roth-Lempel codes, constructed in 1989, are a well-known family of non-Reed-Solomon MDS codes valued for their algebraic structure, low-complexity decoding, and applications in cryptography and data storage, motivating the search for new twisted variants with controlled parameters.
method: The authors construct a class of twisted Roth-Lempel codes and analyze their algebraic and coding-theoretic parameters, deriving necessary and sufficient conditions for minimum distance n-k or n-k+1 and for MDS/NMDS status, using Schur square dimension arguments to distinguish them from Reed-Solomon and original Roth-Lempel codes.
result: They fully characterize when TRL codes achieve minimum distance n-k or n-k+1 and when they are MDS or NMDS, and prove the Schur square of a TRL code has dimension at least 2k+1, establishing inequivalence to the corresponding RL code and non-Reed-Solomon status.
conclusion: The twisted Roth-Lempel construction yields a new family of non-Reed-Solomon codes with well-determined distance and MDS/NMDS properties, extending the classical Roth-Lempel family and enriching the landscape of MDS codes for cryptographic and storage applications.

title: Constructions Of LCPs And Lcd Codes From Twisted Reed-Solomon Codes
authors: Shuo Sun, Wenwen Chen, Chao Liu, Yaozong Zhang, Xiaoqiang Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear complementary pairs (LCPs) and linear complementary dual (LCD) codes have important applications in orthogonal direct-sum masking (ODSM), which provides effective countermeasures against side-channel attacks and fault-injection attacks. While LCD codes have been extensively investigated, comparatively fewer results are available for general LCPs. In this paper, we further investigate LCPs of twisted Reed--Solomon (TRS) codes. We derive necessary conditions for two TRS codes to form an LCP and establish several sufficient conditions and explicit constructions. We also study LCD codes constructed from TRS codes and investigate the security parameters of the resulting LCPs. Furthermore, under suitable conditions, we obtain MDS LCPs of TRS codes.
tldr: The paper constructs linear complementary pairs (LCPs) and linear complementary dual (LCD) codes from twisted Reed-Solomon (TRS) codes, deriving conditions and security parameters for applications in orthogonal direct-sum masking.
motivation: LCPs and LCD codes are useful for side-channel and fault-injection countermeasures via orthogonal direct-sum masking, but general LCP constructions from TRS codes remain less explored than LCD codes.
method: The authors derive necessary conditions for two TRS codes to form an LCP, establish sufficient conditions and explicit constructions, and analyze security parameters; they also obtain MDS LCPs under suitable conditions.
result: They provide several sufficient conditions and explicit constructions of LCPs and LCD codes from TRS codes, and show that MDS LCPs can be obtained under suitable conditions.
conclusion: The work extends the theory of LCPs and LCD codes using TRS codes, offering new designs with potential cryptographic masking applications, though it remains within classical coding theory.

title: A Multiuser Channel Capacity Region
authors: John M. Cioffi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A finite structural characterization of the [MATH]-user multiuser channel-capacity region appears here. This region relies upon three concepts: (i) subset-based message atomization, (ii) synchronized receiver chain-rule/Fano reduction, and (iii) successive-decoding achievability via a finite-super-symbol closure. The resulting region is a finite union of order-indexed polytopes parameterized by the synchronized minimum mutual-information vector [MATH]. The framework removes auxiliary-random-variable proliferation and makes explicit the finite geometric structure underlying general multiuser converses, with the interference channel providing the primary illustration. For the linear matrix Gaussian multiuser-channel special case under per-user trace covariance constraints, Gaussian signaling is capacity-region-achieving within this framework. Also shown is that maximum rate sum for any Gaussian multiple-user-channel derives from simple iterative procedures.
tldr: A finite structural characterization of the multiuser channel-capacity region is given via message atomization, chain-rule/Fano reduction, and successive-decoding achievability, yielding a finite union of order-indexed polytopes.
motivation: Classical multiuser channel-capacity regions (e.g., interference channels) traditionally require auxiliary random variables, obscuring the underlying geometric structure and making converses unwieldy.
method: The paper introduces subset-based message atomization, a synchronized receiver chain-rule/Fano reduction, and a finite-super-symbol closure to establish successive-decoding achievability; Gaussian signaling is analyzed under per-user trace covariance constraints.
result: The capacity region is expressed as a finite union of order-indexed polytopes parameterized by a synchronized minimum mutual-information vector, with Gaussian signaling shown to be capacity-region-achieving in the linear matrix Gaussian special case, plus simple iterative procedures for maximum rate sum.
conclusion: The framework removes auxiliary-random-variable proliferation and makes explicit the finite geometric structure of general multiuser converses, but it is a classical network information-theory result without quantum extension.

title: Highly Parallel Real-Space Random Phase Approximation Using Lanczos Quadrature And Interpolation
authors: Abir Haque, Edmond Chow, Shikhar Shah, Andrew J. Medford, John E. Pask, Phanish Suryanarayana
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a highly parallelizable, matrix-free, real-space method for computing the random phase approximation (RPA) correlation energy within Kohn-Sham density functional theory. In particular, we avoid the explicit construction and eigen-decomposition of the response function matrix and use Lanczos quadrature to evaluate the trace of a matrix function on a real-space grid. We also show it is possible to exploit the spatial smoothness of the RPA correlation energy density in real-space to reduce computational cost. Specifically, we compute the energy density on a coarse grid, then reconstruct an approximation to the full, fine grid via interpolation. We implement this formulation within the SPARC electronic structure package and demonstrate its convergence, accuracy, agreement with planewave results, and scaling. Interpolation can enable an [MATH] reduction in the computational prefactor. Given the embarrassingly parallel nature of the proposed method, we achieve near-ideal speedups and near-cubic scaling, thus allowing us to compute the RPA correlation energy for a silicon system with 256 valence electrons at chemical accuracy in less than 30 minutes on 4,096 CPU cores.
tldr: The paper introduces a highly parallel, matrix-free real-space method for computing the random phase approximation (RPA) correlation energy in Kohn-Sham density functional theory using Lanczos quadrature and spatial interpolation.
motivation: Computing the RPA correlation energy conventionally requires explicit construction and eigendecomposition of the response function matrix, which is prohibitively expensive for large systems; the authors aim to make such calculations feasible at scale.
method: They avoid building the response matrix by using Lanczos quadrature to evaluate the trace of a matrix function on a real-space grid, and exploit spatial smoothness of the RPA energy density by computing it on a coarse grid and interpolating to the fine grid, implemented in the SPARC electronic structure package.
result: The method shows good convergence, accuracy, and agreement with planewave results, achieving near-ideal parallel speedups and near-cubic scaling, computing the RPA correlation energy of a 256-valence-electron silicon system to chemical accuracy in under 30 minutes on 4,096 CPU cores.
conclusion: Spatial interpolation can reduce the computational prefactor by an order of magnitude, making large-scale RPA calculations practical on modern parallel hardware.

title: Geometric View Of Iterative Fixed-Node Dynamics
authors: Bryan K. Clark Pranav Kairon
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The sign-structure of a quantum many-body ground state is a central quantity in fixed-node approaches to mitigating the Fermion sign problem. For continuum electronic-structure Hamiltonians, the correct sign-structure is sufficient to compute exact ground state properties; on the other hand, lattice fixed-node approaches retain an additional dependence on trial wave-function amplitudes which are improved upon non-optimally while preserving their sign structure. Here we consider an iterative map obtained by repeatedly replacing the fixed-node trial state with the ground state of its associated lattice fixed-node Hamiltonian (independent of whether and how a practical algorithm could implement this iteration). We show the fixed points of this map are eigenstates of the Hamiltonian and reduced Hamiltonian resulting in at most one fixed point in the interior of each sign chamber. We prove that the ground state fixed point is stable and that the boundary of the ground state sign chamber is repulsive. This shows the amplitude dependence beyond having the correct ground state sign-structure disappears under self-consistent iteration. In other sign chambers, energy descent can be obstructed by the imposed sign structure; this tension leads to the iteration driving select amplitudes to zero producing `support collapse' onto chamber boundaries and corresponding to reduced Hamiltonians. Excited-state fixed points are therefore provably unstable and flow toward lower-energy boundary fixed points. We show sign chamber boundaries have a directional stability; boundary points attractive in one direction are repulsive under a sign flip. By revealing the geometry and stability structure of iterative fixed-node dynamics, our results clarify the foundations of a central approach to the Fermion sign problem and motivate potential new algorithmic strategies.
tldr: The paper geometrically analyzes an iterative fixed-node map for lattice Hamiltonians, showing that fixed points correspond to eigenstates and have stability properties tied to sign chambers.
motivation: Fixed-node approaches to the fermion sign problem depend on trial wave-function amplitudes and sign structure; understanding the iteration's fixed points can clarify the foundations and limitations of such methods.
method: The authors define an iterative map that replaces the fixed-node trial state with the ground state of the associated lattice fixed-node Hamiltonian and study its fixed points, stability, and boundary behavior within sign chambers.
result: The fixed points are eigenstates, with at most one interior fixed point per sign chamber; the ground-state fixed point is stable and its sign-chamber boundary is repulsive, while excited-state fixed points are unstable and flow toward lower-energy boundary fixed points via support collapse.
conclusion: The work reveals a geometric stability structure underlying iterative fixed-node dynamics, clarifying amplitude dependence beyond sign structure and motivating new algorithmic strategies.

title: Implementing A White-Box Undetectable Backdoor For Random Fourier Features
authors: Michael Collins, Jada Cumberland, Brianne Dunn, Ross Gore, Samuel Jackson, Sachin Shetty
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Goldwasser et al. showed that undetectable backdoors can be planted in machine learning models trained with the Random Fourier Features (RFF) algorithm, under a hardness assumption tied to the Continuous Learning With Errors (CLWE) problem. Under standard cryptographic assumptions, even a full white-box audit of a model's weights cannot detect this class of backdoor. The construction is stated in terms of cryptographic reductions and probabilistic lemmas, without a reference implementation, and relies on secondary machinery such as the Sparse Gaussian Pancakes distribution and a homogeneous CLWE conditional density. Its realizability in ordinary numerical code is not obvious from the paper alone. This paper implements the white-box CLWE-RFF backdoor construction end to end using only numpy and scipy, to test whether this threat is realizable with commodity scientific-computing tools or requires specialized cryptographic infrastructure. We give two samplers for the core [MATH] distribution. The first is a rejection-sampling proxy. The second is an exact closed-form sampler derived from the homogeneous CLWE density and verified against its own analytic form. Using this implementation, we run statistical indistinguishability tests, covering both weight-space and functional black-box comparisons. We find no evidence of detectable difference between backdoored and clean models across a range of sparsity ratios [MATH]. We report which parts of the construction were straightforward to realize, which required derivation not spelled out in the paper. We also highlight which parts we did not attempt to reproduce, including the underlying lattice hardness reduction. We see this work as a contribution to understanding the practical realizability of the Goldwasser white-box CLWE core, not as a new theoretical result.
tldr: The paper provides a numpy/scipy reference implementation of the CLWE-based white-box undetectable backdoor previously proposed for Random Fourier Features models, testing its practical realizability.
motivation: Goldwasser et al. proposed undetectable backdoors for RFF-trained models based on the Continuous Learning With Errors (CLWE) hardness assumption, but only gave a cryptographic reduction without any implementation, leaving its practical realizability unclear.
method: The authors implement the white-box CLWE-RFF backdoor end to end using only numpy and scipy, providing both a rejection-sampling proxy and an exact closed-form sampler for the core distribution, then run statistical indistinguishability tests in weight space and functionally.
result: No detectable difference between backdoored and clean models was found across a range of sparsity ratios, and the authors document which construction steps were straightforward, which required new derivations, and which (lattice hardness reduction) were not reproduced.
conclusion: The threat is realizable with commodity scientific-computing tools, and the work serves as a practical realizability study of the Goldwasser white-box CLWE construction rather than a new theoretical result.

title: Investigating Interacting Fermionic Models With Locality-Preserving Qubit Encodings
authors: Ashutosh P. Tripathi, Debasish Banerjee, Sandip Maiti, Nilmani Mathur
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the utility of the locality-preserving Derby-Klassen (DK) fermion-to-qubit mapping [arXiv:2003.06939] for variational quantum simulation of two-dimensional [MATH]-[MATH] and Fermi-Hubbard models. The DK mapping preserves the locality of fermionic interactions with an enlarged Hilbert space, thereby requiring additional constraints that define the physical sector. We incorporate these constraints directly into a Hamiltonian Variational Ans\"atz (HVA) through Clifford-gate state preparation and use the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) to show that the low-energy properties of the resulting qubit Hamiltonian are accurately reproduced. We further exploit particle-number conservation inherent in the ans\"atz to resolve distinct symmetry sectors and reliably access degenerate states. Consequently, we benchmark the DK-HVA against Jordan-Wigner-based variational circuits at nonzero chemical potential, where particle-hole symmetry and the associated half-filled sign-free condition are absent. Finally, we demonstrate the advantage of locality-preserving mappings in higher-dimensional fermionic systems, where the conventional Jordan-Wigner (JW) transformation generates increasingly long Pauli strings and corresponding circuit overheads. We further extend the framework to the spinful Fermi-Hubbard model and identify a tradeoff between fermionic-mode placement and the locality of hopping and on-site interaction terms. These results establish a practical framework combining locality-preserving fermion-to-qubit mappings, constraint-preserving Clifford state preparation, and symmetry-preserving variational circuits, that trades auxiliary-qubit and stabilizer-preparation overhead for reduced operator nonlocality, providing a practical route toward resource-efficient quantum simulation of higher-dimensional interacting fermionic systems.
tldr: The paper investigates locality-preserving Derby-Klassen fermion-to-qubit encodings for variational quantum simulation of two-dimensional fermionic models, including Fermi-Hubbard.
motivation: Conventional Jordan-Wigner mappings generate increasingly long Pauli strings and circuit overhead for higher-dimensional fermionic systems, motivating locality-preserving encodings despite auxiliary-qubit costs.
method: The authors use the Derby-Klassen mapping with constraint-preserving Clifford state preparation and a Hamiltonian Variational Ansatz solved via VQE, benchmarking against Jordan-Wigner-based circuits at nonzero chemical potential.
result: The DK-HVA accurately reproduces low-energy properties, resolves symmetry sectors and degenerate states, and shows advantages for higher-dimensional systems while revealing a tradeoff between fermionic-mode placement and locality in the spinful Fermi-Hubbard model.
conclusion: The work establishes a practical framework combining locality-preserving fermion-to-qubit mappings, constraint-preserving Clifford state preparation, and symmetry-preserving variational circuits for resource-efficient quantum simulation.

title: Why Are We Unrolling? The Importance Of Structured Quantum Programs For Compilation
authors: Damian Rovara, Daniel Haag, Mark Koch, Josh Izaac, Seyon Sivarajah, Robert Wille, August\'in Borgna, Lukas Burgholzer, Brad Chase, Olivia Di Matteo, David Ittah
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As quantum software stacks scale up to support future fault-tolerant quantum hardware and algorithms, quantum compilation is becoming an increasingly important component of the stack. How do we ensure that our software stacks support dynamic algorithms, including patterns such as mid-circuit measurement feedforward and repeat-until-success, with hundreds of logical qubits and billions of quantum operations? To do so, we must re-think how we represent quantum programs beyond straight-line circuits, to representations that include classical structure and dynamism, and make this the default representation to consider when performing quantum compilation. In this work, we present important patterns and algorithms from fault-tolerant quantum applications which admit a structured representation that we argue is crucial to preserve, and set a challenge to the community to compile such representations without unrolling them into straight-line quantum circuits. We also explore the status quo of structured program support in quantum software, and ask ourselves the rhetorical question: how much more efficient can we make quantum compilation tooling when we take into account the additional information from classical structure?
tldr: The paper argues that quantum compilation should preserve structured classical control and dynamism in program representations rather than unrolling them into straight-line circuits.
motivation: As quantum software stacks scale toward fault-tolerant hardware and dynamic algorithms, current compilation approaches based on straight-line circuits become inefficient and limited.
method: The authors identify important patterns and algorithms from fault-tolerant quantum applications that admit structured representations, survey the status quo of structured program support in quantum software, and pose a community challenge to compile without unrolling.
result: They show that structured representations carry additional classical information that can significantly improve compilation efficiency, and highlight gaps in existing tooling.
conclusion: The paper calls for rethinking quantum program representations to make structured, dynamic programs the default for compilation in future quantum software stacks.

title: Deterministic Ground-State Search In A Spatial Photonic Ising Machine By Phase Retrieval
authors: Suguru Shimomura, Jun Tanida, Yusuke Ogura
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A spatial photonic Ising machine (SPIM) solves large-scale combinatorial optimization problems by computing the Ising Hamiltonian through an optical Fourier transform. However, the ground-state search relies on the annealing process, in which spins are optimized stochastically and sequentially. We propose a ground-state search based on phase retrieval (PR), in which all spins are updated simultaneously and deterministically. By imposing an amplitude constraint in the Fourier plane, the modulated phase distribution corresponding to a spin configuration is guided toward the optimal solution. We numerically demonstrate that the proposed scheme reaches the ground state of rank-one Ising Hamiltonians with [MATH] spins in a single iteration for all trials. Moreover, a radial rearrangement of the amplitude and the suitable design of the target pattern relaxed the search stagnation and promoted the optimization of spin configurations. The collective and deterministic spin update by phase retrieval provides a fast ground-state search for large-scale combinatorial optimization.
tldr: A spatial photonic Ising machine is proposed to perform deterministic ground-state search using phase retrieval, updating all spins simultaneously.
motivation: Spatial photonic Ising machines typically rely on stochastic and sequential annealing for ground-state search, which limits speed and efficiency.
method: The scheme imposes an amplitude constraint in the Fourier plane to guide the modulated phase distribution corresponding to a spin configuration toward the optimal solution, using phase retrieval for deterministic collective spin updates.
result: Numerical simulations show the proposed scheme reaches the ground state of rank-one Ising Hamiltonians with M spins in a single iteration for all trials, and radial rearrangement of amplitude plus suitable target pattern design relaxes search stagnation.
conclusion: The collective and deterministic spin update via phase retrieval provides a fast ground-state search for large-scale combinatorial optimization.

title: Gauge: A Formal Framework For Measuring Cryptographic Security Under Heterogeneous Adversary Cost Models
authors: Sanjeev Rana Bhanwar Gupta
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standards bodies report cryptographic security as a single number of bits, but this value depends on the adversary cost model used to price time, memory, and quantum resources. Different conventions can therefore produce different rankings of cryptographic schemes. GAUGE represents security as a function over admissible cost models, called a security profile. Comparisons then become comparisons between profiles, and ranking reversals become an explicit structural property rather than a measurement error. We formalize price functionals over a cone of adversary cost models, show that security profiles are piecewise-linear and concave, and prove a rating trilemma: when two profiles cross, no rating can simultaneously be faithful to underlying costs, total over comparable pairs, and independent of the chosen cost model. We provide a polynomial-time linear-programming procedure that certifies whether the ranking of two schemes is robust, reverses under admissible models, or is genuinely incomparable. We extend GAUGE with a two-layer risk measure combining stochastic cryptanalytic decay with uncertainty over the appropriate cost model. We evaluate the framework on NIST post-quantum standards, classical anchors, and a 25-year chronology of cryptanalytic breaks. The analysis certifies a ranking reversal for ML-KEM-512 versus AES-128 from a 4-5% shift in memory pricing, and measures a lattice-sieving cost drift of 9.79 bits per year over eight years. A hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768 handshake reduces combined-break probability twenty-fold at a 2.3 kilobyte cost. The artifact reproduces all tables and figures in under seven seconds. GAUGE provides an explicit and auditable framework for reporting cryptographic security under competing cost models.
tldr: GAUGE formalizes cryptographic security as a function over adversary cost models, enabling certification of whether scheme rankings are robust, reversed, or incomparable.
motivation: Single-number security ratings obscure dependence on adversary cost conventions, allowing different but admissible cost models to produce different rankings of cryptographic schemes.
method: The paper defines price functionals over a cone of cost models, shows security profiles are piecewise-linear and concave, proves a rating trilemma, and provides a polynomial-time linear-programming procedure for ranking certification, plus a two-layer risk measure.
result: It certifies a ranking reversal between ML-KEM-512 and AES-128 under a 4-5% memory-price shift, measures lattice-sieving cost drift of 9.79 bits per year.

title: Beyond Phase Reduction: Amplitude Collapse In Optimal Control Of Coupled Oscillators
authors: Faranak Rajabi, Fr\'ed\'eric Gibou, Jeff Moehlis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We solve the four-dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation for two diffusively coupled Stuart-Landau-like oscillators to obtain full-state optimal feedback control. A sweep over coupling strength reveals a sharp change in the numerically optimal strategy: below a threshold coupling value, the controller steers the phase difference toward anti-phase while keeping both oscillators near the limit cycle, as reduced-order models would suggest. Above this threshold, the HJB solution changes qualitatively; the controller transiently collapses one oscillator's amplitude to near zero, thereby enabling large phase repositioning near the origin before rebuilding its amplitude. Direct gradient-based and stochastic optimization do not recover this lower-cost collapse trajectory from the initializations considered, suggesting that it occupies a region of the control landscape that is difficult to access by direct search. A joint sweep over nonisochronicity and coupling shows that collapse can occur even for an isochronous oscillator: phase repositioning near the origin can favor an off-cycle strategy. Nonisochronicity provides an additional energetic benefit through a phase-velocity surplus at small amplitude, quantitatively accounting for the observed reduction in control cost. Comparisons with uncoupled and coupled phase-reduced baselines show that phase models become increasingly inaccurate and cost significantly more energy for strong coupling. Results for coupled Van der Pol oscillators further demonstrate that exploitation of off-cycle dynamics is not specific to the Stuart-Landau-like oscillators.
tldr: The paper solves the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation for coupled Stuart-Landau oscillators, revealing that optimal control can transiently collapse one oscillator's amplitude to enable cheaper phase repositioning at strong coupling, beyond what phase-reduced models predict.
motivation: Standard phase-reduction methods for controlling coupled oscillators may miss off-cycle strategies that lower energy cost, especially when coupling is strong and phase models become inaccurate.
method: They numerically solve the four-dimensional HJB equation for two diffusively coupled Stuart-Landau-like oscillators, sweep coupling strength and nonisochronicity, and compare with gradient-based and stochastic optimization as well as uncoupled and coupled phase-reduced baselines, also testing Van der Pol oscillators.
result: Above a threshold coupling, the optimal controller transiently collapses one oscillator's amplitude near zero, enabling large phase repositioning near the origin at lower cost; nonisochronicity provides additional energetic benefit via a phase-velocity surplus at small amplitude.
conclusion: Optimal control of coupled oscillators can exploit off-cycle dynamics that phase-reduced models fail to capture, and phase models become increasingly inaccurate and energetically costly for strong coupling.

title: Boundedness In Strict Deformation Quantization
authors: Michael Heins
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper provides a complex-analytic interpretation of certain topologies on the tensor algebra, which are a central tool within strict deformation quantization. We prove that the symmetric tensor algebra [MATH] of a barelled nuclear DF-space [MATH] endowed with any of these topologies may be understood as an algebra of bounded Fr\'echet holomorphic functions on the strong dual space [MATH]. The coarsest of the topologies then corresponds to the topology of uniform convergence on bounded subsets. The finer ones provide an infinite-dimensional generalization of the order of an entire holomorphic function. To facilitate these results, we study the interplay between boundedness and continuity of holomorphic mappings between locally convex spaces. As a byproduct, we establish a simple sufficient criterion for Fr\'echet holomorphy as well as several completeness results for spaces of bounded functions.
tldr: The paper gives a complex-analytic interpretation of topologies on the tensor algebra used in strict deformation quantization, identifying the symmetric tensor algebra with algebras of bounded Fréchet holomorphic functions on the strong dual space.
motivation: Strict deformation quantization relies on certain topologies on the tensor algebra, but their analytic meaning has not been clarified; the author aims to characterize them via complex analysis on locally convex spaces.
method: The author studies boundedness and continuity of holomorphic mappings between locally convex spaces for barrelled nuclear DF-spaces, and relates the tensor-algebra topologies to uniform convergence on bounded subsets and to an infinite-dimensional notion of the order of an entire function.
result: The symmetric tensor algebra with these topologies is shown to consist of bounded Fréchet holomorphic functions, with the coarsest topology corresponding to uniform convergence on bounded sets and finer ones generalizing the order of entire functions; a sufficient criterion for Fréchet holomorphy and completeness results are also obtained.
conclusion: The work provides a functional-analytic foundation for topologies in strict deformation quantization, but remains a pure-mathematics contribution without direct bearing on quantum information, thermodynamics, or quantum networks.

title: Observational Indistinguishability And Integrity Blind Regions In Hybrid Quantum-Classical Workflows
authors: Roberto Fern\'andez-Barrios, Iker Pastor-L\'opez, Amaia Pikatza-Huerga, Pablo Garc\'ia Bringas
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17150v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a claim-relative evidence/reference framework for hybrid quantum-classical workflow integrity. Observational indistinguishability yields structural blind regions, distinct from finite-batch statistical misses. Within the declared lattice, a trusted same-batch scalar [MATH] suffices for conclusion integrity, aggregate [MATH] for aggregate plus conclusion integrity, and item-aligned binding for item identity. In 3,600 label interventions, feature/prediction views realize exact label-path invariance; all 764 geometry-aligned aggregate-blind rows equal their paired-clean responses, giving zero attack-only increment. For statistical response, the geometry-aligned construction detects 343/2,700 conclusion-changing ([MATH]) label interventions with the conformal rule and 1,183/2,700 with the uncorrected union; the original frozen same-item geometry yields 11/2,617 and 43/2,617, respectively. The executed conformal clean false-action rates are 0.048--0.059 descriptively; its finite-sample guarantee requires exchangeability, which the overlapping-draw design violates. The cluster-preserving adaptive stress test (Gate A) reduces response versus matched controls in 25--40 of 40 environment/split cells while retaining conclusion changes. A bounded 165-design-cell ideal-statevector and finite-shot-emulation branch directly instantiates semantic, estimated and observed kernel transitions. The fixed equal-weight design estimates neither deployment prevalence nor QPU, provider or deployed-service assurance.
tldr: The paper introduces a claim-relative evidence framework that identifies structural blind regions in hybrid quantum-classical workflow integrity, where observational indistinguishability can prevent certain aggregate checks from detecting label interventions.
motivation: To assess and defend the integrity of hybrid quantum-classical workflows against adversarial or accidental label interventions that may be hidden by observational equivalence.
method: The approach defines a claim lattice and uses same-batch scalars, aggregate/item-aligned binding, label interventions, conformal detection rules, cluster-preserving adaptive stress tests, and a bounded ideal-statevector/finite-shot emulation branch.
result: Geometry-aligned aggregate-blind rows equal paired-clean responses with zero attack-only increment; conformal detection finds 343/2700 conclusion-changing label interventions versus 1183/2700 for uncorrected union, with clean false-action rates 0.048–0.059; the stress test reduces response in 25–40 of 40 cells.
conclusion: The framework characterizes integrity blind spots and detection limits in hybrid quantum-classical workflows, but it does not estimate deployment prevalence, QPU, provider, or deployed-service assurance.

title: Euclidean Svp Is NP-hard For Cyclic Lattices
authors: Daqing Wan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that exact Euclidean SVP is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions for full-rank cyclic integer lattices, equivalently full-rank ideals of [MATH] in the coefficient norm. Hardness holds with [MATH] for a varying odd prime [MATH]. As an application, we prove the same hardness for the algebraic class of NTRU-form lattices [MATH], where [MATH] are unrestricted inputs. The decision problems are NP-complete, and the exact search problems are NP-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. No hardness claim is made for cryptographic NTRU parameter subclasses or key-generation distributions.
tldr: The paper proves that exact Euclidean SVP is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions for full-rank cyclic integer lattices, and extends the hardness to NTRU-form lattices.
motivation: Lattice problems underpin post-quantum cryptography, but hardness results have largely been established for general lattices; whether structured (cyclic/ideal) lattices retain comparable hardness is an important complexity-theoretic question.
method: The author works with full-rank cyclic integer lattices, equivalently full-rank ideals in a number ring under the coefficient norm, and derives deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions for a varying odd prime, with translated arguments for NTRU-form lattices.
result: Exact Euclidean SVP is NP-hard for cyclic lattices and for NTRU-form lattices with unrestricted inputs; the corresponding decision problems are NP-complete and the exact search problems are NP-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions.
conclusion: The work places structured cyclic and NTRU-form lattices in the same hardness class as general lattices, though no hardness claim is made for cryptographic NTRU parameter subclasses or key-generation distributions.

title: Cybersecurity In Power Grids: Standards And Research Challenges
authors: Ferran Bohigas-Daranas, Hamid Latif-Martinez, Nicolas Llorens, David Bru I Bru, Oriol Gomis-Bellmunt, Eduardo Prieto-Araujo, Pere Barlet-Ros
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper examines Smart Grid cybersecurity, emphasizing the critical distinctions between IT and OT environments. It analyzes grid architecture, substation threats, and key international standards, specifically IEC 62351, IEC 62443, and ISO 27001. Finally, it overviews latest research trends, including AI-driven threat detection.
tldr: A survey of Smart Grid cybersecurity covering IT/OT distinctions, grid architecture, substation threats, and standards such as IEC 62351, IEC 62443, and ISO 27001, along with emerging research trends like AI-driven threat detection.
motivation: Power grids are increasingly digitized and interconnected, exposing operational technology to cyber threats that traditional IT security frameworks handle poorly, motivating a dedicated review of standards and open challenges.
method: Structured survey and comparative analysis of grid architectures, substation-level threat models, and international cybersecurity standards, complemented by an overview of current research directions.
result: The paper identifies gaps between IT and OT security requirements, catalogs relevant standards and their scope, and highlights AI-based threat detection as a prominent emerging research area.
conclusion: Effective Smart Grid security requires OT-aware standards and cross-disciplinary research, with AI-driven detection and standards harmonization identified as key priorities.

title: Tight Lower Bounds For Algebraic Communication And Applications
authors: Manon Blanc, Prateek Dwivedi, Magnus Rahbek Dalgaard Hansen, Nutan Limaye, Meena Mahajan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Communication complexity studies how much information must be exchanged to solve a problem whose input is split among several parties. The classical setting deals with Boolean inputs split between two parties. We study an algebraic variant, where the inputs are vectors over a field [MATH]. Alice and Bob have inputs [MATH] and [MATH], respectively. We consider two kinds of tasks: the polynomial evaluation problem (compute the value of a polynomial [MATH]), and the set-recognition problem (decide whether (X,Y) is in [MATH], for [MATH]). In both settings, Alice and Bob send evaluations of polynomials depending only on their own inputs. In the set-recognition problem, a referee receives the messages and may apply polynomial tests to the messages received so far; the outcomes of these tests determine acceptance or rejection. The protocols may be deterministic or probabilistic. We study: - Upper bounds and reductions: We give non-trivial upper bounds for a range of natural polynomial evaluation and set-recognition problems and prove reductions between different problems, which help organize the landscape of the model. - A lower bound framework and tight lower bounds: Our main technical contribution is a general framework for proving lower bounds for algebraic set-recognition problems. We prove several probabilistic lower bounds for natural problems, giving tight or near-tight characterizations of their algebraic communication. - Applications of the framework: Finally, we give two applications of our framework: proving lower bounds for a class of left-to-right algebraic algorithms (algebraic scanners) and a more general algebraic computational setting inspired by the BSS model.
tldr: The paper develops a lower-bound framework for algebraic communication protocols where parties send polynomial evaluations, with applications to algebraic scanners and BSS-model computation.
motivation: Communication complexity studies information exchange, and the authors extend it to an algebraic setting over fields, aiming to characterize the cost of polynomial evaluation and set-recognition tasks under deterministic and probabilistic protocols.
method: They give upper bounds and reductions between algebraic communication problems, then introduce a general framework for proving probabilistic lower bounds via polynomial tests applied by a referee.
result: The framework yields tight or near-tight lower bounds for natural algebraic set-recognition and polynomial-evaluation problems, and it is applied to lower bounds for left-to-right algebraic scanners and a BSS-inspired computational model.
conclusion: This is a contribution to classical algebraic communication and computational complexity, not directly connected to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Formalization Of Sullivan's No Wandering Domains Theorem In Lean
authors: Yusheng Luo Ziang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report on a Lean 4 formalization of Sullivan's No Wandering Domains theorem: every Fatou component of a rational self-map of the Riemann sphere of degree at least two is eventually periodic. The project formalizes the relevant background in normal families, the Montel-Carath\'eodory theorem, Julia and Fatou sets, local Sobolev regularity and Wirtinger derivatives, the Cauchy and Beurling transforms, the equivalence of analytic and geometric quasiconformality, and the measurable Riemann mapping theorem. This paper describes the translation of this mathematics into Lean, the proof architecture, the reusable components, and the autoformalization workflow.
tldr: The paper reports a Lean 4 formalization of Sullivan's No Wandering Domains theorem for rational self-maps of the Riemann sphere, covering normal families, quasiconformality, and the measurable Riemann mapping theorem.
motivation: The authors aim to demonstrate that a substantial theorem in complex dynamics can be fully formalized in a proof assistant, thereby providing reusable verified components for mathematical analysis in Lean.
method: The work translates complex-analytic background—Montel-Carathéodory, Julia/Fatou sets, Sobolev regularity, Wirtinger derivatives, Cauchy and Beurling transforms, analytic-geometric quasiconformality equivalence, and the measurable Riemann mapping theorem—into Lean 4, using an autoformalization workflow.
result: A complete Lean 4 formalization of Sullivan's No Wandering Domains theorem is achieved, along with a description of the proof architecture and reusable formalized components.
conclusion: The paper contributes to the formalization of complex dynamics and proof-assistant methodology, but has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Maxwell-J$\"u$ttner Averaged Nonaffine Theory Of Relativistic Shear Viscosity
authors: Ali \"ovg\"un Reggie C. Pantig
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate a Maxwell-J\"uttner averaged extension of relativistic nonaffine shear-viscosity theory for a classical gas of massive particles. The starting point is the relativistic nonaffine response formula derived from generalized Langevin dynamics, where proper-momentum dissipation produces a Lorentz-factor enhancement of the viscosity. Since a thermal relativistic gas is not characterized by a single Lorentz factor, we replace this scalar enhancement by an equilibrium momentum average over the Maxwell-J\"uttner distribution. Within the scalar transverse mean-field closure used in this work, the minimal relativistic correction is the Maxwell-J\"uttner mean of the Lorentz factor and becomes a finite-mass enhancement function of [MATH]. In the general closure, the averaged object is the full product of the Lorentz factor, the zero-frequency memory kernel, and the nonaffine affine-force correlator. This construction separates kinematic relativistic enhancement from dynamical dissipation encoded in the bath memory and collective mode spectrum. We derive the nonrelativistic and ultrarelativistic limits, show that a specified effective hard-sphere scaling reproduces the classical square-root law as a consistency test, and identify the assumptions under which a cubic high-temperature law follows. Comparison with relativistic kinetic-theory examples clarifies that the memory kernel is not equivalent to a relaxation time unless a microscopic closure is specified. Retaining the full frequency dependence instead yields a relaxation spectrum. A single dominant pole reduces this spectrum to one shear relaxation time and gives the usual transient shear equation.
tldr: The paper formulates a Maxwell-Jüttner averaged nonaffine theory of relativistic shear viscosity for a classical gas of massive particles.
motivation: A thermal relativistic gas does not have a single Lorentz factor, so the scalar Lorentz-factor enhancement of viscosity from nonaffine response theory must be replaced by an equilibrium momentum average.
method: The authors average the relativistic nonaffine response formula from generalized Langevin dynamics over the Maxwell-Jüttner distribution, using both a scalar transverse mean-field closure and a general closure involving the full memory kernel and affine-force correlator.
result: The minimal correction is the Maxwell-Jüttner mean of the Lorentz factor, while the general closure yields a product of the Lorentz factor, zero-frequency memory kernel, and nonaffine correlator; nonrelativistic and ultrarelativistic limits are derived, and an effective hard-sphere scaling reproduces the classical square-root law.
conclusion: The construction separates kinematic relativistic enhancement from dynamical dissipation, clarifies that the memory kernel is not generally equivalent to a relaxation time, and shows that a single dominant pole reduces the relaxation spectrum to the usual transient shear equation.

title: A Programmable Optics Cloud Laboratory
authors: Sachin Vaidya, Caio Silva, Seou Choi, Joshua Chen, Marin Solja\v{c}i\'c
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laboratory automation can improve experimental throughput, accessibility, and reproducibility, but many robotic laboratory systems remain difficult to reconfigure. This challenge is especially pronounced in free-space optics, where experiments are built from heterogeneous components, require precise alignment, and are frequently rearranged as experimental goals change. In this work, we present the Programmable Infrastructure for Cloud Optics (PICO), a robotic cloud-laboratory architecture designed to make reconfigurable optical experiments easier to program, operate, and reproduce. PICO provides a common domain-specific abstraction and software layer through which experimental configurations and actions can be controlled across different user interfaces.
