tldr: This paper presents an agentic LLM-based framework that automatically detects potential log file exposures in third-party WordPress CMS plugins using static and dynamic analysis.
motivation: CMS plugins often create insecure log files that leak credentials and personal data, yet log file exposure remains an understudied attack surface despite powering roughly 58% of the web.
method: The authors build an autonomous LLM agent that inspects each plugin via static and dynamic analysis, and they evaluate it on the 300 most-installed WordPress plugins (over 250M active installations), manually validating every finding.
result: They reproduced 79 of 81 findings across 62 plugins, identified creation-control and access-control protection patterns, and derived a taxonomy of log file path and protection schemes with best-practice recommendations.
conclusion: The study shows that multi-layered protection is required but inconsistently present, and that agentic LLMs are a useful tool for security analysis of plugin ecosystems.

title: Universal Properties Of Petri Net Unfoldings
authors: Hugo Paquet Serge Lechenne
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is an established idea in concurrency theory that every Petri net admits an unfolding semantics. This is a denotational object that represents its domain of possible executions. Unfoldings play an important role in practical analysis and verification. This paper is concerned with the following well-known problem: while the unfolding resembles a universal construction in the category of Petri nets, it generally fails to satisfy the expected universal property. This is because the unfolding construction overlooks the net's internal symmetries. There are two solutions: make these symmetries explicit to obtain a weak universal property (one that holds only ''up to symmetry''); or break the symmetries by assigning individual identities to components of the net. We review these two solutions and establish, in each case, a universal unfolding of Petri nets to event structures. This paper demonstrates a 2-categorical approach to Petri net unfoldings. We show that each unfolding semantics determines a 2-categorical relative adjunction involving Petri nets and event structures. Viewed in this way, the above two constructions can be related formally via an appropriate morphism of adjunctions. We exhibit a 2-density property of event structures which implies that unfolding functors are essentially unique.
tldr: This paper develops a 2-categorical framework for Petri net unfoldings to event structures, showing that unfolding semantics determine relative adjunctions and that a 2-density property of event structures forces unfolding functors to be essentially unique.
motivation: While Petri net unfoldings resemble universal constructions in the category of Petri nets, they generally fail to satisfy the expected universal property because the construction ignores internal symmetries of the net.
method: The authors review two remedies—making symmetries explicit for a weak universal property, or breaking symmetries via individual component identities—and formalize both using a 2-categorical relative adjunction between Petri nets and event structures, related by a morphism of adjunctions.
result: Each unfolding semantics yields a 2-categorical relative adjunction, and a 2-density property of event structures implies essential uniqueness of the unfolding functors.
conclusion: The 2-categorical perspective clarifies the universal structure of Petri net unfoldings and unifies the two symmetry-handling approaches, though the work lies in concurrency theory rather than quantum information.

title: Living Structure + Ai: A New Episteme For Liberal Arts And Whole-Person Education In The Era Of Artificial Intelligence
authors: Bin Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education signals an epistemic shift in how knowledge is created, taught, and evaluated. This paper argues that Christopher Alexander's theory of living structure offers a timely foundation for liberal arts and whole-person education in the AI era. Living structure is understood through two inseparable dimensions: living, the intuitive perception of wholeness, and structure, the underlying order that can be analyzed through fifteen geometric properties, two fundamental laws, two design principles, and the computable L- and B-scores. Building on this foundation, the paper proposes Living Structure + AI as a new episteme for higher education. The ordering is deliberate: living structure is more fundamental, while AI serves as a tool for perceiving, measuring, and generating it. The argument draws on teaching by LivableCityLAB in partnership with Residential College 1, including architecture and city-science courses, an undergraduate common-core course, and a postgraduate experiential-learning course. Across four campus-renovation projects and two courses involving 89 students, participants learned to read environments structurally, establish a design skeleton, and use AI as a structural mediator. L- and B-scores increased in every renovation, broadly converging with preference tests and visual-attention analysis. Course assignments provided additional, though not psychometrically validated, evidence of student engagement. The paper concludes that the deepest contribution of Living Structure + AI lies not on screens, but in enabling students to feel, measure, and remake wholeness in everyday spaces.
tldr: The paper proposes 'Living Structure + AI' as a new episteme for liberal arts and whole-person education, grounded in Christopher Alexander's theory of living structure and illustrated through campus-renovation projects and courses.
motivation: The rapid integration of AI into higher education is shifting how knowledge is created, taught, and evaluated, creating a need for a pedagogical foundation that keeps human perception of wholeness central rather than subordinated to AI tools.
method: The authors build on Alexander's living structure theory—defined by fifteen geometric properties, two laws, two design principles, and computable L- and B-scores—and apply it in teaching via LivableCityLAB in four campus-renovation projects and two courses with 89 students, using AI as a structural mediator.
result: L- and B-scores increased in every renovation, broadly converging with preference tests and visual-attention analysis, and course assignments offered additional though not psychometrically validated evidence of student engagement.
conclusion: The deepest contribution of Living Structure + AI lies not on screens but in enabling students to feel, measure, and remake wholeness in everyday spaces.

title: How To Build A Campfire? Participatory Modelling With Justice
authors: Nynke van Uffelen, Sander Ten Caat, Aarthi Sundaram, Annemiek de Looze, Marion Collewet, Eefje Cuppen, Igor Nikolic
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energy transition decision-making is pervaded by deep uncertainties. Computational models are helpful in addressing such uncertainties, as they can give insight into techno-economic complexity. However, models alone are insufficient, as part of the uncertainties involve justice dilemmas.
tldr: This paper proposes a participatory modelling approach that integrates justice considerations into computational models used for energy transition decision-making under deep uncertainty.
motivation: Energy transition decisions involve deep uncertainties that computational models can help address in techno-economic terms, but models alone cannot capture the normative justice dilemmas embedded in such decisions.
method: The authors develop a participatory modelling methodology ('How To Build A Campfire') that combines computational modelling with stakeholder deliberation to surface and address justice concerns.
result: The approach is presented as a framework for jointly exploring techno-economic complexity and justice dilemmas in energy transition planning.
conclusion: Integrating justice into participatory modelling yields more legitimate and robust decision support for energy transition governance under uncertainty.

title: Higher-order Interactions Reveal Synergistic Backbones Of Cycling Infrastructure Networks
authors: Christoph Steinacker, Henrik Wolf, Marc Timme, Malte Schr\"oder
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Infrastructure networks essentially underlie human mobility and transport. Improving the quality of single links increases network performance locally. However, efficient transport requires high-quality connected corridors across multi-link paths that do not emerge from independent single-link upgrades. Here, we introduce a framework for evaluating the impact of jointly upgrading multiple links as inherently higher-order interactions, enabling us to quantify link synergies in complex transport networks. Two links are synergistic if an upgrade of one increases the benefit of upgrading the other, promoting upgrades of topologically complementary links along the same path while discouraging upgrades of redundant parallel links. By expressing these synergies as second-order derivatives of overall network performance, we develop an efficient computational framework to identify synergistic links that form a connected network backbone. We apply our theoretical framework by combining empirical street network and cycling demand data for Hamburg, Germany, with a perturbed utility route choice model for urban bicycle traffic. Our results reveal synergies from higher-order interactions, thereby enabling strategic infrastructure planning that goes beyond local link importance in complex transport and flow networks.
tldr: The paper introduces a framework for quantifying synergistic higher-order interactions between links in transport networks and applies it to cycling infrastructure planning in Hamburg.
motivation: Efficient transport requires coordinated multi-link upgrades rather than independent single-link improvements, motivating a method to identify synergistic link combinations.
method: The authors express link synergies as second-order derivatives of overall network performance and combine empirical street network and cycling demand data with a perturbed utility route choice model.
result: They identify synergistic links forming a connected backbone, showing that joint upgrades can outperform local link-importance assessments and reveal complementary corridors.
conclusion: Higher-order interaction analysis enables strategic infrastructure planning beyond local link importance, though the work is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Unified Framework For Measuring Segregation Resolves How Social And Geographical Space Jointly Shape Connections
authors: Johannes Happenhofer, Sahil Loomba, Till Hoffmann, Sumeet Agarwal, Nick S. Jones
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Our understanding of how geographical and social segregation interact remains limited, as relatively few studies investigate them jointly, and existing approaches often lack a framework distinguishing geographical, social, and total segregation. Additionally, large-scale individually resolved geo-social network data are rarely publicly available. We address both. Conceptually, we develop a unified framework that measures segregation in geosocial networks by comparing network models to appropriate null models and recovers the Theil index, dissimilarity index, and network modularity as special cases. Empirically, we turn to privacy-preserving aggregated relational data (ARD): we combine the Facebook Social Connectedness Index for the US with US Census and Pew data, and introduce an ARD-compatible joint geosocial intervening-opportunities model to infer link probabilities between region--group cell pairs. Applying our segregation framework, we find that social segregation predominates over geographical segregation, with notable separation for White--Black, college-degree--no-degree, and high-income--low/middle-income across both segregation types. We find increasing social homophily with geographical distance and group-specific geographical connectivity patterns, suggesting that geographical segregation may affect cross-group connectivity not only directly but also by amplifying social segregation.
tldr: The paper introduces a unified null-model-based framework for measuring social and geographical segregation in geosocial networks, applied to Facebook and Census data to show social segregation dominates over geographical segregation in the US.
motivation: Few studies jointly analyze geographical and social segregation, and existing approaches lack a principled framework that distinguishes geographical, social, and total segregation, partly because large-scale geo-social network data are rarely available.
method: The authors develop a framework that measures segregation by comparing network models against appropriate null models, recovering the Theil index, dissimilarity index, and network modularity as special cases, and introduce an ARD-compatible joint geosocial intervening-opportunities model applied to Facebook Social Connectedness Index data combined with US Census and Pew data.
result: Social segregation is found to predominate over geographical segregation, with pronounced separation along White–Black, college-degree–no-degree, and income lines, and social homophily increases with geographical distance while group-specific geographical connectivity patterns emerge.
conclusion: The unified framework clarifies how social and geographical space jointly shape connections, suggesting geographical segregation affects cross-group connectivity both directly and by amplifying social segregation.

title: Study Of The Algebra Of Smooth Integro-differential Operators With Applications
authors: Adel Kassaian Ahmad Haghany
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the algebra of integro-differential operators with smooth coefficients and kernels on a subspace of [MATH]. We find a normal form for elements of this algebra and determine its unit group. The formulation of inverses gives explicit solutions of inhomogeneous linear Volterra integro-differential equations and Volterra integral equations of first kind with smooth kernels.
tldr: The paper studies the algebra of smooth integro-differential operators on a function space, deriving a normal form, determining its unit group, and using explicit inverses to solve Volterra integro-differential and first-kind integral equations.
motivation: Integro-differential operators appear throughout analysis and applied mathematics, but their algebraic structure (units, normal forms, invertibility) is not fully understood, which limits systematic solution methods for related equations.
method: The authors work on a subspace of smooth functions with smooth coefficients and kernels, establishing a normal form for algebra elements and characterizing the unit group; inversion formulas are then translated into solution schemes for inhomogeneous linear Volterra equations.
result: A normal form for smooth integro-differential operators is obtained, the unit group of the algebra is determined, and explicit solution formulas for Volterra integro-differential equations and first-kind Volterra integral equations with smooth kernels are given.
conclusion: The algebraic approach yields concrete and constructive solution procedures for classes of Volterra equations, illustrating how operator-algebra structure organizes classical integral-equation theory.

title: Immensely Questionable Tests
authors: Siyona Agarwal, Julian Bernhoft, Karam Gill, Yonis Gulleth, Eric Huang, Benjamin Li, Brandon Ni, Soham Samanta, Leone Seidel, Boya Yun, Tanya Khovanova
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study self-referential multiple-choice tests in which the answer choices are positive integers and the question asks how many answer choices are correct. These tests quickly lead to several kinds of ambiguity and paradox. The paper presents the ideas through a dialogue between Queen Tanya and her ten sages, developing a framework for studying these immensely questionable tests.
tldr: The paper analyzes self-referential multiple-choice tests whose positive-integer answer choices ask how many choices are correct, exposing ambiguities and paradoxes through a dialogue between Queen Tanya and ten sages.
motivation: Self-referential test questions of the 'how many answers are correct' form are notoriously confusing and paradoxical, motivating a systematic study of their logical structure.
method: The authors develop a framework for classifying such tests, illustrating the resulting ambiguities and paradoxes via a narrative dialogue between a queen and her ten sages.
result: The analysis delineates several distinct kinds of ambiguity and paradox that arise in these self-referential tests and provides a framework for reasoning about them.
conclusion: Self-referential multiple-choice tests are 'immensely questionable' objects whose logical pitfalls can be systematically characterized through the proposed framework.

title: Isometric Copies Of $\ell_\infty^n$ In Lipschitz-free Spaces Over Finite Metric Spaces
authors: Rainis Haller
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For every [MATH], we construct a finite metric subspace [MATH] of [MATH] such that the Lipschitz-free space [MATH] contains a linear isometric copy of [MATH]. This answers a question posed by Khan, Mim, and Ostrovskii, who obtained examples in dimensions three and four. As a consequence, the finite-dimensional real Banach spaces that admit a linear isometric embedding into a Lipschitz-free space over a finite metric space are precisely the polyhedral spaces.
tldr: The paper constructs finite metric spaces whose Lipschitz-free spaces contain linear isometric copies of ℓ∞^n, answering a question of Khan, Mim, and Ostrovskii and characterizing the finite-dimensional Banach spaces that embed isometrically into such free spaces.
motivation: The problem concerns which finite-dimensional real Banach spaces can be linearly and isometrically embedded into Lipschitz-free spaces over finite metric spaces, a question previously resolved only in low dimensions.
method: The author constructs, for every n, a finite metric subspace of some Euclidean space such that its Lipschitz-free space contains a linear isometric copy of ℓ∞^n.
result: This yields the characterization that exactly the polyhedral finite-dimensional real Banach spaces admit linear isometric embeddings into Lipschitz-free spaces over finite metric spaces.
conclusion: The work settles the open problem and completes the classification of finite-dimensional Banach spaces isometrically embeddable into Lipschitz-free spaces over finite metric spaces.

title: Transfinite Contractive Propagation And The Ball Fixed Point Property In \texorpdfstring{$C(K)$}{C(K)}
authors: Cleon S. Barroso
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that, for a compact Hausdorff space [MATH], the real Banach space [MATH] has the ball fixed point property if and only if [MATH] is extremally disconnected. The new implication is obtained by constructing a fixed-point-free nonexpansive self-map of the whole closed unit ball whenever [MATH] is a compact [MATH]-space which is not extremally disconnected. The construction uses a transfinite contractive propagation system with two increasing profiles. A successor--limit delay preserves their tail constraint and has no subsolution in the profile domain. Analysis records boundary deficits; positive operators on ordinal [MATH]-spaces and a common center determined by the two tails yield a nonexpansive synthesis satisfying an order domination inequality. The required topological families are obtained from a gap in a maximal Boolean chain in the zero-dimensional case, and from a transfinite extension of signs otherwise. The argument works in ZFC and resolves the question posed by Avil\'es, Jap\'on, Lennard, Mart\'inez-Cervantes, and Stawski.
tldr: The paper characterizes when the real Banach space C(K) has the ball fixed point property, proving it holds if and only if K is extremally disconnected.
motivation: The ball fixed point property for C(K) spaces was an open question posed by Avilés, Japón, Lennard, Martínez-Cervantes, and Stawski.
method: The proof constructs a fixed-point-free nonexpansive self-map of the closed unit ball using a transfinite contractive propagation system with two increasing profiles and a successor-limit delay, combining positive operators on ordinal spaces and topological families from maximal Boolean chains or transfinite sign extensions.
result: It is shown that C(K) has the ball fixed point property exactly when K is extremally disconnected, resolving the open problem in ZFC.
conclusion: The work settles the characterization of the ball fixed point property for C(K) spaces, with techniques based on transfinite propagation and order domination.

title: Physics Informed Random Feature Neural Networks For Solving PDEs
authors: Chi-An Chen, Chunyang Liao, Ming Zhong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning-based partial differential equations (PDEs) solvers have attracted significant attention in recent years. Most progress in this area has been driven by deep neural networks such as physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and kernel method (such as physics-informed Gaussian Processes). We introduce a physics-informed random feature method for countering part of the spectral bias which PINN-based solvers are facing for a certain class of PDEs. Random feature method was originally proposed to approximate large-scale kernel machines and can be viewed as a specialized randomized neural network. Compared to other state-of-the-art PINN-based solvers which require a large number of collocation points, our proposed method reduces the computational complexity. In this paper, we develop a rigorous approximation error analysis and derive high-probability error bounds on the [MATH] norm. We provide extensive numerical tests for verifying our theoretical guarantees on error decay rates, as well as several comparison tests to showcase our claimed capability for combating spectral bias in these deep learning based methods.
tldr: This paper introduces a physics-informed random feature method for solving partial differential equations, with rigorous approximation error bounds and numerical tests showing reduced spectral bias compared to PINNs.
motivation: Deep learning PDE solvers such as PINNs suffer from spectral bias and require many collocation points, motivating more efficient alternatives.
method: The authors develop a randomized neural network based on random features, derive high-probability error bounds in a suitable norm, and validate the approach numerically.
result: The proposed method reduces computational complexity relative to state-of-the-art PINN-based solvers and demonstrates improved mitigation of spectral bias for certain PDE classes.
conclusion: Random feature neural networks provide a theoretically grounded and efficient alternative for physics-informed PDE solving, though the work is purely classical and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Structure-Informed Data-Driven Reduced-Order Modeling Of Scalar Hyperbolic Conservation Laws Via Kinetic Defect Measure
authors: Marissa Llamas, Jan Fuhg, Hannah Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reduced-order modeling of transport-dominated systems remains challenging because moving fronts and shocks are poorly represented by low-dimensional linear subspaces. We develop a structure-informed data-driven reduced-order model(ROM) for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws based on the kinetic defect formulation. This formulation separates the nonlinear dynamics into known characteristic transport and a kinetic entropy defect localized on the shock manifold. We exploit this structure by first removing the known transport from the solution snapshots. We then extract and register the remaining defect-driven dynamics in a shock-attached coordinate system. Separate ROMs are used to evolve the shock geometry and the registered defect-driven source. During prediction, the predicted shock geometry is used to inverse-register the learned defect-driven source, which advances the kinetic state and recovers the physical solution. Numerical examples in one and two spatial dimensions demonstrate accurate reconstruction and prediction of nonlinear transport with shocks, including evolution beyond the training interval, while accurately capturing the mass and entropy-dissipation behavior of the reference solution.
tldr: Develops a structure-informed data-driven reduced-order model for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws by using a kinetic defect formulation to separate transport and shock-localized dynamics.
motivation: Reduced-order modeling of transport-dominated systems is difficult because moving fronts and shocks are poorly captured by low-dimensional linear subspaces.
method: The authors remove known characteristic transport from solution snapshots, then extract and register the remaining kinetic entropy defect in a shock-attached coordinate system, evolving shock geometry and defect-driven source with separate ROMs.
result: Numerical examples in one and two spatial dimensions accurately reconstruct and predict nonlinear transport with shocks, including extrapolation beyond the training interval while preserving mass and entropy-dissipation behavior.
conclusion: The proposed structure-informed ROM provides an effective framework for modeling shock-dominated scalar conservation laws, though it is unrelated to quantum information science.

title: Characterizing Heterogeneous Rates In Finite Mixture Estimation Via Partial Optimal Transport
authors: Dung Le, Huy Nguyen, Trang Pham, Alessandro Rinaldo, Nhat Ho
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameter estimation in finite mixture models can exhibit highly heterogeneous convergence behavior: locally isolated components may be estimated substantially faster than groups of competing components. Existing analyses based on Wasserstein distances typically characterize only the worst-case rate and therefore do not fully capture this local heterogeneity. In this paper, we introduce a Voronoi-based partial optimal transport (VPOT) framework for obtaining refined local and global convergence guarantees for the maximum likelihood estimator of the mixing measure. The key geometric idea is to localize the comparison of two mixing measures to extended Voronoi neighborhoods and use partial optimal transport to accommodate the unequal masses of their local restrictions. Within each neighborhood, the first-order POT discrepancy is raised to a power determined by the number of locally competing atoms, allowing the resulting loss to adapt to the local degree of singularity. Under suitable regularity and strong identifiability conditions, we establish uniform local and global upper bounds for a maximum likelihood estimator under the VPOT loss. These bounds reveal a configuration-dependent form of parameter estimation: less singular local configurations admit faster convergence, whereas the most singular configuration recovers the classical worst-case behavior characterized by Wasserstein-based analyses. We further establish a minimax lower bound showing that the convergence rate for estimating the mixing measure under the VPOT loss is optimal. Our results hold in arbitrary fixed dimension without requiring mixing proportions to be uniformly bounded away from zero or prior knowledge of the true number of mixture components. Overall, VPOT provides a configuration-adaptive framework for capturing heterogeneous parameter-estimation behavior in finite mixture models.
tldr: The paper introduces a Voronoi-based partial optimal transport framework for characterizing heterogeneous convergence rates in finite mixture model estimation.
motivation: Existing Wasserstein-based analyses only capture worst-case convergence rates and fail to reflect local heterogeneity in estimating mixture components.
method: It localizes comparisons of mixing measures to extended Voronoi neighborhoods and uses partial optimal transport to handle unequal masses, with exponents determined by the number of locally competing atoms.
result: The authors establish uniform local and global upper bounds for the maximum likelihood estimator under the VPOT loss, and prove a minimax lower bound showing the rate is optimal.
conclusion: VPOT provides a configuration-adaptive framework for capturing heterogeneous parameter-estimation behavior in finite mixture models, without requiring uniformly bounded mixing proportions or known component count.

title: Marginal Maximum Likelihood Estimation And Asymptotic Theory For Latent Variable Models In High Dimensions
authors: Gongjun Xu Chengyu Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work addresses a longstanding gap in the statistical foundations of marginal maximum likelihood estimation for high-dimensional latent variable models. Marginal maximum likelihood estimation is widely used to fit latent variable models across the social sciences, ecology, and machine learning. Despite its broad use, rigorous asymptotic theory for nonlinear models remains limited when both the sample size and the number of observed variables diverge. The gap arises largely from the fact that integration over the latent variables creates a nonlinear objective that tightly couples the high-dimensional model parameters. To address this issue, we first show that the marginal likelihood exhibits multiple nearly flat directions even at the true parameter, in contrast to the behavior in the fixed-dimensional case. Building on this geometric characterization, we develop new techniques to establish consistency and asymptotic normality for the marginal estimator of the high-dimensional parameters. For the latent variables, we provide frequentist and Bayesian uncertainty quantification, proving asymptotic normality of the maximum a posteriori estimator and a Bernstein-von Mises-type result for the plug-in posterior. Together, these results provide rigorous foundations for marginal estimation and latent-variable inference in high-dimensional models.
tldr: This paper develops asymptotic theory for marginal maximum likelihood estimation in high-dimensional latent variable models, addressing consistency, asymptotic normality, and uncertainty quantification.
motivation: Marginal maximum likelihood is widely used for latent variable models, but rigorous asymptotic theory is lacking when both sample size and number of observed variables diverge.
method: The authors characterize the geometry of the marginal likelihood, showing multiple nearly flat directions even at the true parameter, and then develop new techniques to establish consistency and asymptotic normality.
result: They prove consistency and asymptotic normality for the marginal estimator of high-dimensional parameters, and provide frequentist and Bayesian uncertainty quantification for latent variables, including asymptotic normality of the MAP estimator and a Bernstein-von Mises result for the plug-in posterior.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous statistical foundations for marginal estimation and latent-variable inference in high-dimensional settings, with potential impact in social sciences, ecology, and machine learning.

title: Penalty-Uniform Localization For State-Constrained Policy Iteration
authors: Yeongjong Kim, Jiwoong Jang, Yeoneung Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Penalizing a state constraint creates a singular localization problem: whole-space values may grow like the inverse penalty parameter, while numerical diffusion allows even an inward feedback to cross the boundary. For deterministic discounted optimal control, we show how the penalty itself supplies confinement that offsets this growth. With mesh size [MATH] and penalty parameter [MATH], an inward barrier bounds the additional cost of numerical leakage by [MATH] for a monotone centered-difference scheme with vanishing viscosity. Under [MATH], an occupation estimate then yields [MATH] localization error with a sufficient box margin logarithmic in [MATH] and independent of [MATH]. We extend the result to bounded squared-distance penalties and combine it with residual-based evaluation bounds and discounted policy-error propagation. Under coupled refinement with vanishing penalization and discretization errors, explicit conditions on evaluation errors and greedy gaps ensure convergence of the neural value approximations to the constrained value, allowing measurable, nonunique greedy selectors. Reference calculations isolate leakage and localization across mesh and penalty scales, and distinguish evaluation, iteration, and approximation errors. An explicit cylindrical state-constraint solution provides a benchmark in arbitrary dimension, tested up to dimension twenty. Paired obstacle-navigation experiments illustrate why policy-value accuracy must be assessed alongside sampled residuals when comparing raw-residual and finite-grid-assisted neural evaluation.
tldr: The paper analyzes penalty-based localization and convergence for state-constrained policy iteration in deterministic discounted optimal control, with numerical and neural approximation guarantees.
motivation: Penalizing state constraints creates a singular localization problem where values can grow with the inverse penalty parameter while numerical diffusion permits boundary leakage.
method: The authors use a monotone centered-difference scheme with vanishing viscosity, occupation estimates, and coupled refinement to bound localization error and extend results to bounded squared-distance penalties.
result: They derive explicit localization error bounds, convergence conditions for neural value approximations, and benchmark a cylindrical state-constraint solution up to dimension twenty.
conclusion: The work provides a framework for assessing policy-value accuracy alongside residuals in constrained policy iteration and obstacle-navigation experiments.

title: Universal Defenses For Tool-Integrated Llm Agents Against Adversarial Attacks
authors: Yunli Wang Xiaoyan Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of domains, particularly when integrated with external tools for multi-step task completion. However, they are increasingly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, including direct prompt injection, indirect prompt injection, memory poisoning, and backdoor attacks, which exploit the model's openness to prompt injection and tool manipulation. In this work, we explore practical and generalizable defense strategies within a unified framework across these four attack types. We introduce two universal tool-based defenses: Attacker Tool Filtering, which uses anomaly detection (e.g., Isolation Forest) to identify and remove suspicious tools, and Normal Tool Recalling, a white-box method that restores the agent's original toolset prior to planning. Additionally, we incorporate prompt-based defenses: Chain-of-Thought prompting and self-reflection techniques to enhance reasoning and task paraphrasing to mitigate attacks. Experimental results across both four open-source LLMs (Gemma2-9B, Qwen2-7B, LLaMA3-8B, and LLaMA3.1-8B) and three proprietary LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and GPT-5) show that our methods significantly reduce the Attack Success Rates (ASR), achieving 0% ASR in many settings, while preserving or even improving the original task success rate. These findings highlight the promise of simple, modular, multi-layered defenses for strengthening the security and robustness of tool-integrated LLM agents. The code is available at [URL].
tldr: The paper proposes universal defenses for tool-integrated LLM agents against prompt injection, memory poisoning, and backdoor attacks.
motivation: LLM agents using external tools are vulnerable to adversarial manipulations, motivating practical defense strategies that generalize across attack types.
method: The authors combine tool-based defenses (Attacker Tool Filtering with anomaly detection and Normal Tool Recalling) with prompt-based defenses (Chain-of-Thought prompting, self-reflection, and task paraphrasing).
result: Experiments on four open-source and three proprietary LLMs show significantly reduced attack success rates, often achieving 0% ASR, while preserving or improving task success.
conclusion: Simple, modular, multi-layered defenses can strengthen the security and robustness of tool-integrated LLM agents.

title: Feasibility Of Homomorphic Inference For A Genomic Foundation Model
authors: Christos Galanopoulos, Kimon Antonios Provatas, Ilias Georgakopoulos-Soares
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human genomic sequences can identify individuals, cannot be replaced after disclosure, and are the inputs that genomic foundation models are designed to interpret. We assess whether a compute provider can execute a released genomic foundation model without receiving query-derived genomic values in plaintext and whether correctness, memory, or cost prevents complete encrypted inference. We first reproduce the released model on three genomic task families and freeze an independently validated numerical reference. We then implement a client-assisted approximate homomorphic encryption protocol: the provider evaluates linear algebra on ciphertexts, while the key-holding data owner evaluates exact normalization, causal softmax, and activation functions at fixed boundaries. A noninteractive configuration completes one released-weight block but exceeds the tested accelerator-memory envelope when configured for composition. The client-assisted configuration executes all released transformer blocks and the task head for one heldout genomic-signal input at its full prompt length. It matches the frozen final label, peaks at 9,839 mebibytes of accelerator memory, and completes in 6,683 seconds on one accelerator. These results establish arithmetic feasibility for a complete classifier, while repeatability, network transport, and private token-index lookup remain unresolved. The biomedical significance is that, under the stated threat model, a served genomic model can process an encoded sequence without exposing plaintext queryderived activations to the compute provider.
tldr: The paper studies feasibility of homomorphic encryption for private inference on a genomic foundation model, showing a complete classifier can run encrypted but with high computational and memory cost.
motivation: Genomic sequences are sensitive and immutable if disclosed, so there is a need to run genomic foundation models without exposing plaintext query-derived genomic values to a compute provider.
method: The authors reproduce a released genomic foundation model, freeze a numerical reference, and implement a client-assisted approximate homomorphic encryption protocol where the provider evaluates linear algebra on ciphertexts and the client handles normalization, softmax, and activations.
result: A noninteractive configuration exceeds tested accelerator memory for composition, while the client-assisted configuration completes all transformer blocks and the task head, matches the frozen label, uses 9,839 MiB accelerator memory, and takes 6,683 seconds on one accelerator.
conclusion: The work establishes arithmetic feasibility for a complete encrypted genomic classifier under a stated threat model, but repeatability, network transport, and private token-index lookup remain unresolved.

title: Analyzing Multi-Factor Authentication Through Cryptographic Security Properties
authors: Ryan Tipping, Yousef Tahboub, Krishna Bodige
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16214v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern authentication systems use cybersecurity techniques to validate the identity of the person (or applications acting on behalf of the person) as a primary defense against unauthorized access. While initially built around single mechanisms such as usernames/passwords, physical tokens, or biometrics, current systems have evolved into multi-factor authentication (MFA) platforms that combine multiple mechanisms. Among them, several focus on strategies that prevent replay attacks (i.e. the reuse of a component that could have been potentially compromised).
tldr: This paper analyzes multi-factor authentication systems through cryptographic security properties, with emphasis on preventing replay attacks.
motivation: Modern authentication systems combine multiple mechanisms, and understanding their cryptographic security properties is important for defending against unauthorized access and replay attacks.
method: The authors survey and analyze MFA strategies, focusing on cryptographic security properties and how different factors prevent replay attacks.
result: The paper characterizes security properties of MFA platforms and identifies strategies that mitigate replay attacks.
conclusion: MFA provides stronger authentication than single-factor methods, but the work is a classical cybersecurity analysis with no direct quantum information or thermodynamics content.

title: RuleAutoPilot: Synthesizing Deployable Suricata Rules From Network Traffic
authors: Mughees Ur Rehman, Aritran Piplai, Murat Kantarcioglu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rule-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) such as Suricata are central to network security, yet crafting effective detection rules demands deep expert knowledge and cannot keep pace with emerging threats. Existing LLM-based approaches can reduce analyst effort, but they either rely on curated threat intelligence that is produced only after the underlying traffic artifacts already exist, or they require costly LLM use without sufficient quality control. We present RuleAutoPilot, an end-to-end agentic framework that generates deployable Suricata rules directly from malware network traffic, with no prior threat intelligence required. A key challenge is noise: network traffic captures often contain a small amount of security-relevant traffic mixed with large volumes of background traffic, which reduces LLM reasoning quality and increases cost. RuleAutoPilot addresses this challenge with a Benign Traffic Fingerprinting stage that removes known benign background flows before LLM processing. Rules that fail syntax checks, do not trigger on the source traffic, or generate false positives on a benign corpus are automatically repaired using structured feedback. Across 1,296 malware PCAPs, execution-grounded verification raises rule quality (F1) from 0.443 to 0.539. On a stratified 200-PCAP subset, RuleAutoPilot on the open-weight gpt-oss-120b reaches near-frontier quality, 0.524 F1 against Claude Opus 5 under Claude Code's 0.623, at 52x lower billed-token cost. Swapping only the backbone to Claude Opus 5, RuleAutoPilot surpasses Claude Code outright, 0.656 F1 against 0.623, at 40x fewer tokens. A stronger backbone raises RuleAutoPilot's own ceiling, but at the same backbone, our scaffold still outperforms Claude Code's, showing the scaffold contributes independently of the backbone.
tldr: RuleAutoPilot is an LLM-based agentic framework that synthesizes deployable Suricata intrusion detection rules directly from malware network traffic without prior threat intelligence.
motivation: Manual Suricata rule creation requires deep expertise and cannot keep pace with emerging threats, while existing LLM approaches rely on curated threat intelligence or costly, poorly controlled LLM use.
method: The framework filters benign background traffic via Benign Traffic Fingerprinting, then uses execution-grounded verification and structured feedback to repair rules that fail syntax checks, do not trigger on source traffic, or produce false positives.
result: Across 1,296 malware PCAPs, rule quality F1 improves from 0.443 to 0.539; on a 200-PCAP subset, RuleAutoPilot with gpt-oss-120b reaches 0.524 F1 versus Claude Code with Claude Opus 5 at 0.623, and swapping to Claude Opus 5 surpasses Claude Code at 0.656 F1 with far lower token cost.
conclusion: The scaffold contributes independently of the backbone, enabling near-frontier rule generation at much lower cost and outperforming a strong baseline when using the same backbone.

title: Evaluating The Nist Bugs Framework Against Cwe As A Successor For Automated Vulnerability Classification
authors: Md Nazmul Hoque, Shaswata Mitra, Subash Neupane, Sudip Mittal, Shahram Rahimi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability classification based on root cause weaknesses is essential for numerous cybersecurity activities, where the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) serves as a public repository of such flaws. However, its overlapping entries create a non-orthogonal structure. The result is the same vulnerability being mapped to multiple weaknesses, complicating Root Cause Analysis (RCA) and triage. To address this, NIST Special Publication 800-231 introduces the Bugs Framework (BF), which organizes vulnerabilities into triples and links such triples into a causal chain, so that a vulnerability carries its root cause and its sink together instead of a single terminal label. To date, however, BF has been specified but not evaluated regarding its performance against the challenges to automated classification. The evidence required for adoption has not been investigated empirically. We evaluate BF as a classification target and a complement to CWE using a systematically screened corpus of automated Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) linked to CWE research. We assess the reproducibility of CVE-to-BF classification through two evaluations. The first is qualitative: an anonymized inter-rater study in which 2 subject-matter experts (SMEs) independently mapped 13 CVEs onto the four BF axes. Annotators showed strong agreement on the cause and operation axes, while the attribute axis indicated fair agreement. We also tested our automated framework across two large language model (LLM) deployments under different budgets for reproducibility analysis. Despite limitations, such as evidence availability and the absence of retrievable fix commits for closed-source software, our findings support the claim that BF is a more structured and automation-friendly framework than CWE. Our exploration reveals specific gaps in BF, including under-specified guidance on attributes.
tldr: This paper empirically evaluates the NIST Bugs Framework as a successor or complement to CWE for automated vulnerability classification, finding BF more structured and automation-friendly.
motivation: CWE's overlapping entries create a non-orthogonal structure that complicates root cause analysis and triage, while BF was proposed as a more structured alternative but had not been empirically evaluated for automated classification.
method: The authors conducted an anonymized inter-rater study with 2 subject-matter experts mapping 13 CVEs onto the four BF axes, and tested an automated classification framework across two large language model deployments.
result: Annotators showed strong agreement on the cause and operation axes and fair agreement on the attribute axis, while LLM-based classification demonstrated reproducibility and supported BF as more automation-friendly than CWE despite gaps in attribute guidance.
conclusion: BF is a more structured and automation-friendly framework than CWE for vulnerability classification, but under-specified guidance on attributes and data limitations remain challenges for adoption.

title: Not All Relations Are Equal: Relation-Balanced And Calibrated Graph Learning For Provenance-Based Intrusion Detection
authors: Lijie Zheng, Ji He, Alessandro Brighente, Yulong Shen, Mauro Conti
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Provenance-Based Intrusion Detection Systems (PIDSs) detect Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) by analyzing system interactions. However, existing methods largely treat relations uniformly, overlooking statistical heterogeneity; in CADETS, relation frequencies differ by approximately [MATH]. This may cause PIDSs to focus more on frequent relations and overlook differences in normal error levels across relations, increasing the risk of false alarms and missed detections. We present RECAL, an unsupervised framework using relation-balanced masked graph learning to better capture rare interaction patterns. It further calibrates reconstruction errors against each relation's benign error distribution to produce comparable anomaly evidence, helping distinguish attacks from benign behavior and reduce false alarms. On three DARPA E3 datasets, RECAL achieves F1 scores of 99.99\%, 99.93\%, and 99.99\%, outperforming the best baseline on each dataset by 0.88, 0.82, and 0.42 percentage points, respectively. Compared with the baseline reporting the lowest FPR, RECAL reduces mean FPR by approximately [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH].
tldr: RECAL is an unsupervised relation-balanced and calibrated graph learning framework for provenance-based intrusion detection that improves anomaly detection performance on DARPA E3 datasets.
motivation: Existing provenance-based intrusion detection systems treat all system interaction relations uniformly, overlooking statistical heterogeneity across relations, which can cause frequent relations to dominate and lead to false alarms or missed detections.
method: The authors propose RECAL, which uses relation-balanced masked graph learning to capture rare interaction patterns and calibrates reconstruction errors against each relation's benign error distribution to produce comparable anomaly evidence.
result: On three DARPA E3 datasets, RECAL achieves F1 scores of 99.99%, 99.93%, and 99.99%, outperforming the best baseline by 0.88, 0.82, and 0.42 percentage points, and reduces mean false positive rates compared with the lowest-FPR baseline.
conclusion: Relation-aware balancing and calibration substantially improve unsupervised provenance-based intrusion detection, but the work is in cybersecurity and graph learning rather than any of the specified quantum research directions.

title: The Mal Simulator: Cyber Operations Simulation Based On Attack & Defense Graphs
authors: Jakob Nyberg, Sandor Berglund, Andrei Buhaiu, Joakim Loxdal, Pontus Johnson, Mathias Ekstedt
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We have developed the MAL Simulator, a cyber operation simulator based on the Meta Attack Language (MAL). The MAL Simulator is intended for decision-driven cyber attack and defense simulations, for system analysis and the development of automated agents. By building the simulator around an attack modeling language, it can be adapted to different target domains without modifying the source code. We used the simulator for two case studies where we trained two types of agents for automated cyber operations: a defensive agent and an offensive agent. To ground the experiments, we base the models in data collected from an emulated network implemented in the cyber range CRATE. We found that the trained attacker policy could reach the designated targets more efficiently than the compared search methods, and that the trained defender agent induced lower costs than a naive heuristic agent under noisy alert conditions. When testing the RL attacker against the RL defender, we found that the performance of the defenders dropped significantly. This emphasizes the importance of cyber attack simulators to facilitate training both offensive and defensive agents. The MAL Simulator and associated tooling is publicly available and provides common interfaces for compatibility with existing machine learning frameworks.
tldr: The MAL Simulator is a cyber operations simulator based on attack and defense graphs for training and evaluating automated offensive and defensive agents.
motivation: Decision-driven cyber attack and defense simulations are needed for system analysis and developing automated agents, and a flexible simulator based on an attack modeling language can adapt to different target domains.
method: The authors build the simulator around the Meta Attack Language (MAL), use it in two case studies to train reinforcement-learning defensive and offensive agents, and ground experiments in data from the CRATE cyber range.
result: The trained attacker policy reached targets more efficiently than compared search methods, and the trained defender induced lower costs than a naive heuristic under noisy alerts, though defender performance dropped significantly against the RL attacker.
conclusion: The work highlights the importance of cyber attack simulators for training both offensive and defensive agents, and the MAL Simulator is publicly available with interfaces for existing machine learning frameworks.

title: From Hypervisor To Container: Cloud Security Vulnerabilities, Defense Mechanisms, And Open Challenges
authors: Swapnil Vishwas Baviskar, Sanoj R, Hiran V Nath
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cloud computing, different users share the same physical hardware, which creates serious security risks. To protect data, cloud systems rely on virtual machines and containers to keep users isolated. This paper reviews over 120 security publications from 2008 to 2025, focusing on how these isolation boundaries can be breached. We examine threats like virtual machine escape, virtual machine hopping, CPU cache side-channels, container breakouts, vulnerable container images, and distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks. We evaluate these security threats and their defenses using three key research questions. To compare different defense systems, we introduce a quantitative scoring framework called ADPO, which rates defenses from 0 to 3 based on their Accuracy, Deployment ease, Performance impact, and Operational overhead. We also map the impact of these attacks onto a 1-to-5 severity scale for Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability. Finally, we highlight the trade-offs between security and system performance, and we outline open challenges like building low-overhead intrusion detection and creating realistic test datasets.
tldr: A review of cloud security vulnerabilities and defenses spanning hypervisor and container isolation, including side-channel, breakout, and DDoS attacks.
motivation: Cloud multi-tenancy relies on virtualization and container isolation, but these boundaries can be breached, creating serious security risks.
method: The authors review over 120 security publications from 2008 to 2025, structure the analysis around three research questions, and introduce an ADPO quantitative scoring framework and a 1-to-5 severity scale for CIA impacts.
result: The paper categorizes threats such as VM escape, VM hopping, CPU cache side-channels, container breakouts, vulnerable images, and DDoS, and compares defenses using ADPO while highlighting security-performance trade-offs.
conclusion: The review outlines open challenges, including low-overhead intrusion detection and realistic test datasets, and emphasizes the need to balance security with system performance in cloud environments.

title: MarkSec: Capability-Aware Evaluation Of Adversarial Attacks Against Llm Watermarks
authors: Kairong Li, Zhikun Zhang, Xiao Ren, Yunjun Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM watermarking helps trace the origin of generated text, but faces stealing attacks that recover watermark information, scrubbing attacks that remove watermark signals, and spoofing attacks that forge text accepted as watermarked. These attacks are often studied in isolation, leaving their connections unclear. Evaluations also often lack shared detector calibration, metric definitions, and reporting protocols. Moreover, measuring attack success and text quality separately makes it difficult to identify attacks that are both effective and quality-preserving. We propose MarkSec, a general framework that unifies analyses of stealing, scrubbing, and spoofing. We evaluate attacks under a common reporting protocol and introduce a quality-constrained attack success metric to assess effectiveness and text quality jointly. Experiments across representative watermark families, attacks, LLMs, and datasets reveal three findings. First, attacks that appear strongest by watermark removal alone can fall behind general rewriting when success also requires acceptable text quality. Second, general rewriting remains a strong baseline across watermark families, while its advantage over other scrubbers varies by family. Third, in a case study of one watermark family, stealing-based scrubbers often underperform the best general-scrubbing baselines when text quality is required. These results show that apparent attack winners depend on text-quality constraints, attack generality, and capability assumptions.
tldr: MarkSec is a unified framework for evaluating stealing, scrubbing, and spoofing attacks against LLM watermarks under a common protocol and a quality-constrained success metric.
motivation: Attacks on LLM watermarks are typically studied in isolation with inconsistent detectors, metrics, and reporting, making it hard to compare their real effectiveness while preserving text quality.
method: The authors propose MarkSec, which standardizes evaluation across watermark families, attacks, LLMs, and datasets, and introduces a quality-constrained attack success metric that jointly measures attack effectiveness and text quality.
result: Experiments show that watermark removal alone can misrank attacks, general rewriting remains a strong baseline across watermark families, and stealing-based scrubbers often underperform the best general-scrubbing baselines when text quality is required.
conclusion: Apparent attack winners depend critically on text-quality constraints, attack generality, and capability assumptions, so watermark security evaluations should adopt unified, quality-aware protocols.

title: Toward Secure AI-Powered Penetration Testing Agents: Security Threats, Guardrails, And Architectural Perspectives
authors: Hiran V Nath Rahul Dev T Y
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-powered autonomous agents are transforming the penetration testing space with dynamic, multi-step offensive security workflows that require minimal supervision by humans. These agents leverage sophisticated reasoning abilities and external security tools to independently carry out reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities, devise exploitation plans, and perform post-exploitation operations. But the ability to have persistent memory, to take actions in the real world, and to do long-horizon reasoning raises qualitatively different security concerns than traditional chat-based LLM systems. Existing guardrail mechanisms for conversational AI may not be sufficient to secure autonomous AI pentesting agents accordingly. To address these issues, we carry out a comprehensive security analysis on autonomous AI-penetration testing agents. We systematically analyse representative agent architectures, characterise their trust boundaries and attack surfaces and propose a threat taxonomy that is aligned with the lifecycle and covers LLM lifecycle attacks, agent-architecture attacks and cross-cutting behavioural attacks. We analyse the limitations of existing guardrail mechanisms, identify key research gaps, and discuss future research directions for developing specialised, context-aware, and architecture-aware guardrails to secure next-generation AI-driven offensive security systems.
tldr: This paper analyzes security threats and guardrail limitations for autonomous AI-powered penetration testing agents, proposing a threat taxonomy and architectural perspectives.
motivation: LLM-powered autonomous agents are increasingly used for offensive security workflows, but their persistent memory, real-world actions, and long-horizon reasoning create security concerns beyond traditional chat-based LLM systems.
method: The authors systematically analyze representative agent architectures, characterize trust boundaries and attack surfaces, and propose a threat taxonomy covering LLM lifecycle attacks, agent-architecture attacks, and cross-cutting behavioral attacks.
result: The analysis identifies limitations of existing conversational AI guardrails and highlights key research gaps for securing autonomous AI pentesting agents.
conclusion: The paper calls for specialized, context-aware, and architecture-aware guardrails to secure next-generation AI-driven offensive security systems.

title: Sema-guard: Semantic And Graph-Based Vulnerability Detection In Assembly Code
authors: Kaan Sulkalar Halil Dursunoglu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.17254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cases where source code is not available, such as malware analysis, firmware analysis, and embedded systems analysis, vulnerability detection in compiled programs has gained importance. Current methods are heavily reliant on syntactical regularities or higher level representations that are vulnerable to changes in the compiler and may not be readily applicable to assembly code.In this article, we present SEMA-GUARD, a framework that uses semantic analysis and graph neural networks to identify flaws in assembly code. The approach improves the representation of control flow graphs by adding information about the program's execution at a lower level of abstraction, including stack manipulations, memory accesses, and data flow. A set based on the Juliet Test Suite was used to evaluate the effectiveness of SEMA-GUARD. In this set, each piece of source code is initially translated into assembly language and then broken down into function-level chunks. The suggested method, which relies only on statistical or structural data, achieves an accuracy of 85.1\% and an F1 score of 0.801, according to the results. Such results imply that including semantic information in graph-based models may be a successful method for identifying vulnerabilities in compiled code.
tldr: SEMA-GUARD is a graph neural network framework that detects vulnerabilities in assembly code by enriching control flow graphs with low-level semantic features such as stack manipulations, memory accesses, and data flow.
motivation: Vulnerability detection in compiled binaries is important for malware, firmware, and embedded systems analysis, but existing methods rely on syntax or higher-level representations that are brittle to compiler changes and not directly applicable to assembly.
method: The authors build function-level control flow graphs from assembly code and augment them with semantic information about execution, then apply graph neural networks to classify vulnerable functions, evaluating on a Juliet Test Suite-derived dataset.
result: SEMA-GUARD achieves 85.1% accuracy and an F1 score of 0.801 using only statistical and structural information from the assembly graphs.
conclusion: Incorporating semantic execution details into graph-based models can effectively identify vulnerabilities in compiled code, suggesting a viable path for binary-level security analysis.

title: A Gradient-Reconstruction Lattice Boltzmann Method For Compressible Navier--Stokes--Fourier Equations
authors: Adrian Kummerl\"ander, Fedor Bukreev, Mathias J. Krause
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reaching compressible flow has usually forced lattice Boltzmann methods to abandon the compact stencil or the strict locality that make them efficient. We give up neither, solving the compressible Navier--Stokes--Fourier equations with a scheme that transports only the conserved mass, momentum and energy. The viscous stress and heat flux depend on gradients of the velocity and temperature. To capture them, existing compressible schemes go beyond a single lattice of the conserved fields. They enlarge the velocity set, carry the stress and heat flux as extra transported fields, place the energy on a separate grid, or give up exact streaming for an off-lattice advection. We instead recover the gradients from the non-equilibrium part of the distributions already present, inside the collision. No field beyond the conserved state is transported, no neighbour is read, streaming stays exact, and every computation runs in single precision. The method carries five fields where a transported-flux scheme carries fourteen, at a fraction of the memory and [MATH] times the throughput. Verified against the exact Sod and Becker shock solutions and a supersonic Taylor--Green vortex, it tracks the direct-numerical-simulation reference on the kinetic energy and stays within the reference-solver spread on both dissipation rates.
tldr: A gradient-reconstruction lattice Boltzmann scheme solves the compressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations on a single compact stencil using only the conserved fields, avoiding transported stress/heat-flux fields.
motivation: Compressible lattice Boltzmann methods typically sacrifice compact stencils, exact streaming, or strict locality (or require double precision and enlarged velocity sets) in order to represent viscous stress and heat flux, hurting efficiency.
method: The viscous stress and heat flux are recovered from the non-equilibrium part of the distribution functions inside the collision operator, so only mass, momentum, and energy are transported, no neighbor reads are needed, streaming remains exact, and all computation runs in single precision.
result: The scheme needs five fields versus fourteen for transported-flux approaches, uses far less memory, and achieves much higher throughput, while matching exact Sod and Becker shock solutions and reproducing DNS reference behavior for a supersonic Taylor-Green vortex.
conclusion: The method offers an efficient, accurate, and compact alternative for compressible flow simulation within the lattice Boltzmann framework, but it lies entirely outside the quantum information, thermodynamics, networking, and hybrid quantum systems scope of the researcher's interests.

title: Implicit Lagrangian Hydrodynamics With High-Order Finite Elements
authors: Julian Andrej, John Camier, Veselin Dobrev, Tzanio Kolev, Boyan Lazarov, Ketan Mittal, Robert Rieben, Brandon Talamini, Vladimir Z. Tomov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an implicit time integration capability for high-order curvilinear finite element Lagrangian hydrodynamics. Starting from an existing explicit formulation, the implicit treatment builds directly on the original discretization and operator structure and does not alter the underlying spatial formulation or physics model. We demonstrate our implementation using the Laghos miniapp, which is built on the MFEM finite element library. To support gradient-based nonlinear solution methods, we compute Jacobian actions automatically using MFEM's [MATH]FEM interface together with Enzyme-based automatic differentiation, and apply the resulting Jacobian in a matrix-free or fully-assembled manner within a Newton-Krylov solver. To ensure robust and differentiable nonlinear solves in the presence of shocks, we introduce a smooth artificial viscosity treatment based on smooth approximations of non-differentiable pointwise operations. The differentiable artificial viscosity presently lacks a limiter to ensure high-order scaling away from shocks, but is sufficient for illustrating the benefits of implicit Lagrangian hydrodynamics. The behavior and performance of the implicit method are demonstrated on several standard benchmark problems. We verify high-order convergence on the smooth Taylor-Green vortex in the absence of artificial viscosity, show correct strong-shock behavior on the Sedov blast problem, and obtain significant improvements in accuracy-per-time-to-solution on the Triple Point problem where explicit stability constraints become increasingly severe for high-order discretizations.
tldr: The paper develops an implicit time-integration capability for high-order curvilinear finite element Lagrangian hydrodynamics, implemented in the Laghos miniapp on top of MFEM and leveraging Enzyme-based automatic differentiation for Newton-Krylov solves.
motivation: Explicit time integration of high-order Lagrangian hydrodynamics becomes severely constrained by stability limits, particularly for strong shocks and high-order discretizations, making implicit methods attractive for improving accuracy per unit time-to-solution.
method: Starting from an existing explicit discretization, the authors add implicit time integration without altering the spatial formulation, computing Jacobian actions via MFEM's FEM interface with Enzyme automatic differentiation and solving with matrix-free or assembled Newton-Krylov, using a smooth artificial viscosity to keep the nonlinear solves differentiable near shocks.
result: High-order convergence is verified on the smooth Taylor-Green vortex without artificial viscosity, correct strong-shock behavior is shown on the Sedov blast problem, and significant accuracy-per-time-to-solution gains are obtained on the Triple Point problem.
conclusion: Implicit Lagrangian hydrodynamics is demonstrated to be practical and beneficial for high-order finite element simulations where explicit stability constraints dominate, though a limiter for the differentiable artificial viscosity remains future work.

title: Does The Problem Of The Nile Have A Solution?
authors: Fran\c{c}ois Ollivier Guillaume Ch\`eze
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The problem of the Nile has been stated by R. Fisher in 1936. This problem concerns the fair division of an agricultural land and is the eponymous problem of a general class of problems on measures and similar regions. In 1938, W. Feller has shown that the general problem has no solution. However, we will show that under a natural hypothesis, the original problem of the Nile is solvable with connected plots.
tldr: The paper revisits Fisher's 1936 'problem of the Nile' and shows that, under a natural hypothesis, the original problem admits a solution with connected plots, despite Feller's 1938 general impossibility result.
motivation: The problem of the Nile is a classical fair-division problem concerning measures and similar regions, and its general unsolvability by Feller left open whether the original formulation could still be solved under reasonable assumptions.
method: The authors analyze the problem using measure-theoretic and geometric arguments, imposing a natural hypothesis to establish the existence of a solution with connected plots.
result: They prove that under the stated natural hypothesis, the original problem of the Nile is solvable and the division can be made with connected plots.
conclusion: The work resolves a long-standing variant of Fisher's problem, showing that a positive answer is possible in the original setting when a natural condition is met.

title: From Umbral Hyperbolic Integrals To A Cotangent Coefficient Formula For The Mittag Leffler Polynomials
authors: Luc Rams\`es Talla Waffo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16092v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let \(g_n(x)\) be the Mittag--Leffler polynomials defined by $[MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH]$ This gives a parallel umbral representation for the beta integrals. The family \(q_m\) is a shifted \(c=-1,\beta=1\) specialization of the classical Meixner family, yielding a beta/Meixner counterpart to the zeta/Mittag--Leffler correspondence.
tldr: The paper derives a cotangent coefficient formula for Mittag-Leffler polynomials via umbral hyperbolic integrals and beta integral representations.
motivation: The authors aim to extend umbral calculus techniques to hyperbolic integrals and to establish a beta/Meixner counterpart to the classical zeta/Mittag-Leffler correspondence.
method: Umbral calculus and special-function identities are used to construct parallel umbral representations of beta integrals, with the family q_m identified as a shifted specialization of the classical Meixner family.
result: A cotangent coefficient formula for the Mittag-Leffler polynomials is obtained, along with an umbral representation of the associated beta integrals.
conclusion: The work establishes a structural link between Mittag-Leffler polynomials, Meixner polynomials, and beta integrals, contributing to classical special-function theory.

title: Multiorder Fractional Operators: The Conformable Multiorder Derivative And Its Associated Multiorder Integral
authors: Carlos E Cadenas R
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a novel class of non-linear multiorder fractional differential operators. First, we provide intuitive and formal justifications for the existence of multiorder differential operators through differential analysis and Omega-derivative formulations. We then define the conformable multiorder derivative as a functional quotient of fractional derivatives and establish its analytical properties rigorously. Furthermore, leveraging fundamental principles of mathematical analysis, we construct its inverse operator, termed the conformable multiorder integral. Detailed step-by-step proofs of all theoretical properties are presented. Illustrative examples and applications to solving elementary multiorder differential equations are thoroughly examined. Finally, comprehensive conclusions and strategic outlooks for prospective research directions are discussed.
tldr: The paper introduces a new class of non-linear conformable multiorder fractional differential operators and constructs their corresponding multiorder integrals, with proofs, examples, and applications to elementary multiorder differential equations.
motivation: The authors aim to extend classical fractional calculus by justifying the existence of multiorder differential operators and providing a rigorous framework for their definition and inversion.
method: They use differential analysis and Omega-derivative formulations to motivate multiorder operators, define the conformable multiorder derivative as a functional quotient of fractional derivatives, and derive its inverse via standard analytic arguments.
result: The conformable multiorder derivative's analytic properties are established with step-by-step proofs, and the associated multiorder integral is constructed and illustrated on elementary multiorder differential equations.
conclusion: The work provides a self-contained mathematical framework for multiorder fractional operators and outlines prospective research directions, but remains purely within pure/applied mathematical analysis.

title: Infinitesimal Dynamical Spectral Rigidity Of The Bunimovich Stadium
authors: Xianghui Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the infinitesimal dynamical spectral rigidity of the circular Bunimovich stadium with sufficiently long flat edges, in the class of domains obtained by replacing its two circular arcs with strictly convex [MATH] arcs and keeping its reflection symmetry across the axis parallel to the flat edges. That is, if a [MATH] one-parameter family in this class passing through the stadium preserves the length spectrum, then its deformation function at the stadium vanishes identically. For flat edges of arbitrary length, the deformation functions of such families still span a finite-dimensional space.
tldr: The paper proves infinitesimal dynamical spectral rigidity for the circular Bunimovich stadium with sufficiently long flat edges within a class of convex-arc deformations preserving reflection symmetry.
motivation: The work addresses how much geometric information is encoded in the length spectrum of chaotic billiard domains, specifically whether deformations can preserve the length spectrum.
method: It studies one-parameter families of domains obtained by replacing the stadium's circular arcs with strictly convex arcs while keeping reflection symmetry, and analyzes the deformation functions under length-spectrum preservation.
result: For sufficiently long flat edges, any such family preserving the length spectrum has an identically vanishing deformation function at the stadium; for arbitrary flat-edge lengths, the deformation functions span a finite-dimensional space.
conclusion: The Bunimovich stadium exhibits infinitesimal dynamical spectral rigidity under the considered perturbations, with a finite-dimensional obstruction space in the general flat-edge case.

title: A Matrix-free Augmented High Order Compact Solver For Variable-Coefficient Biharmonic Problems
authors: Jin Li, Kejia Pan, Xu Qian, Li-Lian Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.16478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an augmented high-order compact finite difference method for biharmonic equations with clamped boundary conditions and variable coefficients. Standard mixed-type formulations introduce an auxiliary variable, but its boundary values are unavailable, leaving the resulting discrete systems globally coupled and difficult to solve at large scales. Our key contribution is the development of a new augmented formulation that treats these unavailable boundary values as additional unknowns, reduces the global coupling to a lower-dimensional Schur complement system, and yields decoupled second-order subproblems. The Schur complement is solved by matrix-free GMRES, while the subproblems are handled by FFT-based fast solvers. The method achieves fourth-order accuracy using compact stencils, and has [MATH] computational complexity, enabling the solution of the biharmonic equation with [MATH] degrees of freedom within several minutes. To the best of our knowledge, this level of computational efficiency has not previously been achieved in either the literature or practice. Using energy estimates and Fourier analysis, we derive a new [MATH]-estimate for Poisson equations with inexact Dirichlet boundary and then prove the convergence of the proposed scheme. We provide ample numerical experiments to confirm the accuracy, efficiency, and further apply the fast and accurate solver to triharmonic equations, high-wavenumber problems, Stokes flow, and plate bending problems.
tldr: The paper develops an augmented high-order compact finite difference method with a matrix-free GMRES solver for variable-coefficient biharmonic problems, achieving fourth-order accuracy and near-linear complexity.
motivation: Biharmonic equations with clamped boundary conditions are important in mechanics and physics, but standard mixed formulations introduce globally coupled systems that are hard to solve at large scales due to unavailable auxiliary boundary values.
method: The authors introduce an augmented formulation that treats unavailable boundary values as extra unknowns, reduces the global coupling to a lower-dimensional Schur complement, and solves the Schur complement with matrix-free GMRES while using FFT-based fast solvers for decoupled second-order subproblems.
result: The method achieves fourth-order accuracy with compact stencils and approximately linear computational complexity, enabling solutions with millions of degrees of freedom within minutes; convergence is proved via energy estimates and Fourier analysis.
